speechtext: It being 11.18 o'clock, pursuant to order made Wednesday, November 28, 1990, it is my duty to interrupt Routine Proceedings and call Government Business No. 24.

The House resumed from Wednesday, November 28, the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Clark (Yellowhead):
That this House, noting that the Government of Iraq has not complied with the United Nations Security Council resolutions concerning the invasion of Kuwait and the detention of third country nationals, supports the United Nations in its efforts to ensure compliance with Security Council resolution 660 and subsequent resolutions.
And on the amendment of Mr. Gray (Windsor West):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "its" and substituting the following:
"current efforts to ensure compliance with Security Council resolution 660 and subsequent resolutions adopted as of 28 November 1990, and that this support shall not be interpreted as approval of the use of Canadian Forces for offensive action without further consultation with and approval by this House."
And on the amendment of Mr. Brewin:
That the motion be amended by adding the following words:
"and further, that this House oppose use of force against Iraq until sanctions and other United Nations measures have had time to

Government Orders
succeed and urges the government to seek amendments to the currently proposed Security Council resolution to that effect."

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the Security Council of the United Nations will vote on a resolution authorizing member states, co-operating with the Government of Kuwait, and I quote from the resolution: "to use all necessary means to uphold and implement Security Council resolution 660, and all subsequent relevant resolutions, and to restore peace and security in the area".
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada will vote, this afternoon, in favour of this resolution of the Security Council because Canadians believe profoundly in the United Nations; Canadians support the rule of international law; and, Canadians understand the need for collective security. Now is the time to vote.
In endorsing this resolution, Canada will join the international community in sending President Hussein a clear message that the time has come to take the United Nations directive seriously. The international community will also be giving him, and this I believe is an important consideration, a very clear signal of a "pause of goodwill", during which time he is encouraged and, indeed, invited to release the hostages and to withdraw his forces from Kuwait.
As President Gorbachev of the Soviet Union stated yesterday: "The fate of Iraq is now in the hands of (President Hussein) and time is expiring". Peace is jeopardized, not by the resolution being discussed at the Security Council of the United Nations this afternoon, but by the actions taken by Iraq during the last four months. Peace would be fatally undermined if nations like Canada failed to take appropriate measures and the United Nations was weakened and diminished.
Although Kuwait is distinct from Canada, geographically, Canadian interests are directly engaged in the conflict there.
The Iraqi invasion of Kuwait is a blatant contravention of the system of international law that Canadians among many others have painstakingly helped to create since the Second World War. In fact, no country has a greater
interest than Canada in the promotion, the defence and the respect of the rule of law.
The objective of that law, in part, is to ensure the security of smaller countries in face of larger neighbours, and to provide the means to settle disputes peacefully.
The invasion of Kuwait puts the concept of collective security, as provided for in the United Nations Charter, to a decisive test. Article 1 of the Charter reads, in part, as follows:
The Purposes of the United Nations are to maintain international peace and security, and to that end: to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace, and for the suppression of acts of aggression or other breaches of the peace-
Those words were incorporated right into the Charter of the United Nations.
Today's UN resolution is not just the culmination of diplomatic activity over the past four months. It is also in some important ways the realization of diplomatic aspirations held by many since the founding of the international organization.
With the end of the Cold War, the international community has the opportunity at last to transform the potential of the United Nations into performance. The visionaries who created the United Nations were idealists, but they were not dreamers.
They were determined: "to make certain," as Mr. Pearson wrote in 1945, "that never again should an aggressor be permitted to strike down one nation after another before the peace-loving nations of the world organize and take concerted action against it".
Let me repeat what Mr. Pearson wrote: "never again should an aggressor be permitted to strike down one nation after another before the peace-loving nations of the world organize and take concerted action against it".
Hear, hear.
the House will join with me today in saluting again the courage and the dedication of these brave young Canadians.
Hear, hear.

The United Nations was prevented by the Cold War from responding to other acts of aggression over the years. But that situation has now changed, in very dramatic and remarkable ways. Witness the extraordinary co-operation between the Soviet Union and the United States in this and other important areas around the world, to witness the progressive and the dynamic attitude of President Gorbachev and contrast that in similarly explosive situations in the past with the attitudes of his predecessors.
This is a unique time in international affairs. Because of that, the situation has now changed. With the end of the Cold War, the United Nations has the opportunity again to act collectively in the defence of the security of its members. The United Nations is acting with prudence and care and it is precisely because of its moderation that the United Nations today deserves Canada's support.
Hear, hear.

What is at stake, Mr. Speaker, is not just the future of Kuwait but also, in many important ways, the future of the United Nations. We know what happened to the League of Nations when it stood by as Mussolini invaded Ethiopia. It was reduced to impotence and to scorn. Men and women around the world who believed in liberty and freedom paid an enormous price as the effectiveness of the League disintegrated.
This cannot and must not be allowed to happen to the increasing and effective moral authority that the United Nations is now bringing in a dozen different ways to questions around the world. This cannot happen. What happened to the League cannot and must not ever be allowed to happen to the United Nations.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the lessons of the past must be learned.
Government Orders
Any weakening of the UN, would engender an escalation of military spending for self-defence around the world and a proliferation of ever more dangerous and destructive arms-in short, the creation of a much more dangerous world.
And we know that Iraq, which is already working on weapons of mass destruction and on the means of delivering them over long distances, would become even more uncontrollable.
Canadian interests in Kuwait and the region go beyond the present and potential military dangers and the preservation of the principle of collective security.
The inalienable human rights of millions of people have been, and are still being, callously overridden by Iraq and countless atrocities have been committed against innocent people.
And the economic impacts of the Gulf crisis have been serious on the people of the energy-poor, heavily indebted countries of the third world and on the reconstruction of the newly liberated countries of Eastern Europe which need additional assistance from countries like Canada and other industrialized countries, assistance that is necessarily fragmented as a result of the entirely unusual circumstances in the Gulf.
So Canadian interests are very much engaged in this issue. Nor is the challenge to those interests and to our basic human values ever likely to be more clear or the need to join in a collective response more compelling. In its contempt for international opinion, the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait is one of the most brazen acts of aggression of our age.
Iraq has inflicted death and destruction on its small neighbour, plundered that country, detained foreigners, including Canadians, against their will and given guest workers, many penniless, the choice of braving the desert in August or starving to death.
Since he first used force to occupy Kuwait in August, he has threatened to invade Saudi Arabia, to attack Israel with chemical and biological weapons, to sponsor terrorism against those who resist his aggression and to destroy the oil fields of the Arabian Peninsula.
And this from a man who started a war with another of his neighbours, Iran, that lasted eight years and cost close to a million lives-almost an entire generation wiped out as a result of an act of aggression. This from a

November 29, 1990
Government Orders
man who used poison gas in that war, including against his own citizens.
What is at stake in the Gulf are the foundations of peace and the norm of civilization. The international community must prevail. It is giving diplomacy every chance to work as it must.
As a member of the United Nations Security Council, Canada has worked hard to help draft and pass a series of principled step-by-step resolutions designed to persuade Iraq to withdraw from Kuwait.
We have helped the United Nations design and implement economic sanctions against Iraq that are the most stringent ever adopted. We have ourselves respected those sanctions scrupulously. Indeed, I think that I indicated earlier to the House that the first implication of the international application of sanctions occurred at the Port of Vancouver where Canada immediately interrupted a possible shipment that would have violated even inadvertently the first orders that emanated from the Security Council.
We have dispatched three warships and a squadron of CF-18 fighter aircraft and approximately 1,700 personnel to resist Iraqi aggression and to enforce the United Nations sanctions.
In the many discussions I have had with President Bush on this subject, I have consistently counselled both restraint in securing Iraq's withdrawal from Kuwait and the need to work at all times within the authority of the United Nations Charter.
Indeed, the New York Times reported in August-I believe on its front page-an important disagreement that took place in respect of an interpretation of article 51 where Canada, through our distinguished ambassador, Yves Fortier, led the fight in the Security Council to insist that the suggestion by the United States that any concept of unilateral action at that point in time must be resisted and that the solidarity that this had engendered at the United Nations must be respected.
I believe that that action taken by the Government of Canada on the instructions of the Secretary of State for
External Affairs to Ambassador Fortier resulted in the solidarity we know today. It was consistent with the finest traditions of Canadian diplomacy.
Hear, hear.

That has been my consistent message as well in discussions with President Gorbachev, former Prime Minister Thatcher, President Mitterrand, Prime Minister Andreotti, Chancellor Kohl and other leaders.
It was also the message conveyed by Mr. Clark in the past few days in his most recent discussions with President Mubarak of Egypt, President Ozal of Turkey, King Hussein of Jordan and Prime Minister Shamir of Israel.
The entire Canadian policy in this regard, Mr. Speaker, has been designed with a peaceful solution in mind: support for the United Nations, implementation of sanctions in Canada itself, increased consultations with world leaders exploring all conceivable avenues toward a peaceful solution, deployment of military support to seek to enforce United Nations sanctions and unrelenting diplomatic efforts to secure the release of all Canadians being illegally held in Iraq.
In our discussions with world leaders, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of National Defence, and I have found a remarkable consensus that the best solution to the crisis in the Gulf is indeed the one that Canada has articulated consistently at the United Nations, namely, a peaceful one.
However, we have also found that a very strong consensus exists to the effect that if peaceful means do not work, recourse would have to be added to other necessary means. While the UN sanctions are undoubtedly being felt by the Iraqi and Kuwaiti people, we have found no widespread confidence that they are sufficient to bring about the desired result: namely, to persuade President Hussein to withdraw his forces from Kuwait.
The situation Canada faces is clear. I can tell you that Canada will stand with the overwhelming majority of the world community, including all of our partners in the Security Council, in giving Saddam Hussein an opportunity to reflect carefully on the consequences of his action and a reasonable timetable to withdraw from Kuwait, but withdraw from Kuwait he must.
Hear, hear.

President Hussein, I very much regret to say, appears to be quite prepared to see his people endure hardship indefinitely so he can hang on to Kuwait. We see no contradiction between continuing to apply pressure through economic sanctions, the action of the United Nations, in other words, giving diplomacy a chance and giving President Hussein a period of time to withdraw from Kuwait.

While the Security Council was passing repeated resolutions ordering Iraq to abandon its conquest of Kuwait, President Hussein formally annexed that country, plundered its wealth, brutalized its people, and tried to erase its very identity.
His response to the world community's repeated urgent demands that he withdraw his forces from Kuwait was to send another 250,000 soldiers to that unfortunate country. And to try to protect himself from harm he has detained thousands of foreigners and, cynically, has used many as human shields at strategic locations. Meanwhile, the suffering of the Kuwait people continues!
And the risk persists of an accidental launch of full-scale war in the most volatile region in the world, with consequences that could engulf everyone.
President Hussein is a man of limited acquaintance with the world outside his own borders. From the beginning he appears to have underestimated what the international reaction would be to his attack on Kuwait.
It seems to take a pretty clear and fothright message Mr. Speaker, to persuade him that times have changed, that the will of the world community will not be thwarted and that he will, one way or another, have to leave Kuwait.

Short of the use of force itself, today's UN Security Council resolution is the strongest possible message the international community can send to him.
Members of this House understand at least as well as anyone that we Canadians are a peaceful people.
In Canada, our national day is a time for picnics and family, not for displays of military might. But we Canadians have also learned the lessons of history. We know that not everyone shares our respect for international
Government Orders
law and for the norms of civilized international behaviour.
As Mr. Pearson pointed out so eloquently: "We have also learned the consequences of appeasement".
We know that if Iraq profits from its aggression, the whole idea of collective security will be fatally undermined and the world will become a much more dangerous place. This cannot be allowed to happen.
The object of the exercise at the United Nations today is peace. Although opposition parties have expressed some concerns, some of which I can understand, I hope all members of the House will support the United Nations resolution today in the interests of international solidarity and in the face of a serious threat to world peace.
The Toronto Star pointed out in its lead editorial this morning, and I quote:
For Canada to vote against such a resolution would be to send the wrong signal to Saddam at a critical stage of this psychological warfare.
It would also break faith with an unprecedented consensus that has emerged on this issue between east and west, Arabs and non-Arabs.
I think The Star has made two very important points. The UN's quite unprecedented achievements need now to be sustained by a solid indication of international support. What gives rise to war, Mr. Speaker, is the collapse of international order, and the collapse of international order comes about when member states allow international law to be violated and the United Nations to be ignored. The integrity of the United Nations and its charter is now at stake, and that integrity must be preserved.
Hear, hear.

We hope for the sake of all concerned that President Hussein heeds the United Nations message and withdraws peacefully. That is Canada's policy. That is Canada's objective at the Security Council today, and that has been the objective of our policy from the very beginning.
We strongly urge President Hussein to do so in the interests of his own people, his own nation, and those of world peace. The choice is entirely his to make. We genuinely hope he reflects carefully and that he chooses wisely.

November 29, 1990
Government Orders
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I consider it a great honour to follow the Prime Minister in this debate. I agree with many of the things that the Prime Minister said in this House. I agree, for example, with what he said about the invasion of Kuwait being a blatant contravention of international law. We on this side of the House agree very strongly with this.
The Prime Minister opened his remarks by saying we must have a collective security and now is the time to vote. Mr. Speaker, what is it we are voting for? Are we voting for the resolution which will be voted upon in the United Nations this afternoon, or are we coming back to this House to vote on the resolution on the floor of this House? I remind the Prime Minister that first and foremost we must vote on the resolution before us in this House. If the Prime Minister would like to send a very strong message to the United Nations to show that we all, in the Canadian tradition, support what the United Nations is doing, his party should have no difficulty supporting the Liberal amendment.
The Prime Minister was not here yesterday. I will just remind him what the Liberal amendment is. It is adding to the end of the government motion, after the word "its" substituting the following:
"current efforts to ensure compliance with Security Council resolution 660 and subsequent resolutions adopted as of 28 November 1990, and that this support shall not be interpreted as approval of the use of Canadian Forces for offensive action without further consultation with and approval by this House."
This is something which the Prime Minister promised us before. Now he is backing away from his promise. As the resolution reads, government representatives are interpreting it differently.
I was here until one o'clock this morning hearing the speeches. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs said on the floor of this House that subsequent resolutions means only resolutions passed to this point. I went to the Concise Oxford Dictionary and looked up the meaning of subsequent. The meaning of subsequent is "of later time or date". In other words, the resolution would read:
That this House, noting that the Government of Iraq has not complied with the United Nations Security Council resolutions
concerning the invasion of Kuwait and the detention of third country
nationals, supports the United Nations in its efforts to ensure
compliance with Security Council resolution 660-
To that point we agree. It would continue:
-and subsequent resolutions.
In other words, the UN can pass resolutions next month or during the summer when this House is not sitting. We know that this Prime Minister will not recall Parliament when we ask the Prime Minister to do it, as we did in the Oka crisis and as we did in the Gulf crisis. We asked day in and day out and Canadians asked: "Please recall Parliament and let us debate it first". The Prime Minister did not recall Parliament. That is why we cannot support such a resolution, because we on this side of the House and Canadians cannot trust this Prime Minister or his government.
"Subsequent resolutions", his own Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, meant only previous resolutions. This morning the Prime Minister said that that includes the motion that will be voted on today. Yesterday there was a different interpretation. Are we to trust this government when this government wants us to vote on this?
If the government wants to send a strong message to the United Nations, let it support our amendment. Then it will send a strong message. There is time to negotiate approval and support for that amendment.
What we heard today is a sabre rattling, gun toting, grenade throwing, Rambo Prime Minister. He talks about collective security, and the only way he sees collective security is with arms. What about using diplomacy? What about giving sanctions more time to work?
The Prime Minister himself said there are signs that sanctions are working. Why do we not give those sanctions more time? How long did it take for the sanctions to take effect in South Africa and in other parts of the world? Here the government is putting a time line.
The resolution at the United Nations has a time line. I believe it is January 15. What happens when that time line is up? What happens then? Is it war? If it is war, what kind of war? Nuclear? Chemical warfare? Is this what the government wants Canadians to get into?
November 29, 1990

The Prime Minister correctly said that when Iran and Iraq went to war a million lives were lost. What a tragedy: one million lives between two countries. How many lives are going to be sacrificed when over 20 countries get involved in war, with chemical warfare and the potential of nuclear warfare? Is that what the Prime Minister wants to commit Canadians to?
The Prime Minister said that the United Nations is acting with prudence and care and deserves our support. Yes, it deserves our support to allow sanctions more time to work. It deserves our support to allow for diplomacy. This party congratulates our ambassador, Yves Fortier. He is an excellent ambassador who knows how to negotiate with other countries through diplomacy, but let us give him more time to do this. Let us not put a time line on it.
What if the diplomacy works in, let us say, February, March or at the end of 1991? Are we limited to this January 15 time line and we go to war? What we heard from the Prime Minister today is a little scary.
This is probably one of the most important debates this House will face for a very long time. In fact, the implications of this debate will stay long after we are gone. We are not debating a simple motion to support or oppose sanctioned military aggression in the Gulf, as the Prime Minister tried to convince us. What we are debating is the future of thousands and potentially millions of people around the world. We are debating the end of the cold war in the context of the new international order. We are debating whether peaceful persuasion and the dollar spent in that persuasion is preferable to offensive military action that far surpasses anything that anyone in this House can conceive.
The purpose of the motion we are debating today is to give our government the go-ahead to vote in favour of a Security Council motion that carries with it an ultimatum. In other words, there will be no more room for negotiation. The die will have been cast, and there will be no turning back. I think it is important to all of us in this House to understand what happens to the role of the Security Council once this motion is passed.
The motion, to begin with, was put forward by the United States. We know that. We do not need a lesson in the motives of the American president. Yes, Mr. Bush
Government Orders
wants Hussein out, and he wants him out now, and we agree with that.
The Middle East is and has been since 1940 of critical interest to the United States. The State Department in the 1940s described the Middle East as being a stupendous source of strategic power and one of the greatest material prizes in world history. Eisenhower himself referred to it as the most strategically important area in the world. But, let there be no misunderstanding: my party also condemns the action of Hussein and calls on him to withdraw Iraqi troops from Kuwait immediately.
The sanctions that are currently in place are strictly a United Nations operation under the supervision of the United Nations 661 committee. Douglas Scott, President of the Markland group, and other disarmament spokesmen confirm that a military action as put forth in this motion and as supported by the Prime Minister, would have no UN supervision.
In fact, the United States has made it very clear that it would not allow a committee such as the one that supervised the sanctions to operate. What this means is that essentially the war would be fought by the U.S. and its allies, with no direction from the UN. It means that the responsibility of dealing with Iraq would be turned over to a group of countries beyond UN control.
If one were to look at how the 661 committee works, one would appreciate the degree of control the committee exerts. Responsible for the supervision of humanitarian supplies of food stuffs and medicine, the committee also directs the way in which aircraft and ships are inspected on the way into the Gulf. It monitors very closely legislation and regulations enacted by member countries in complying with the sanctions. Countries with inadequate legislation or regulations are required to respond directly to this committee.
The UN charter, however, does allow for supervision of military action by a military staff committee. Just as recent as last week, I understand, the Soviet Union was hesitant in supporting the resolution unless there was such a committee. This shows that there is a will to pursue courses of action other than by military force.
Unfortunately, the United States has shown, on more than one occasion, that it is able to circumvent quite deliberately any action that it does not consider conducive to U.S. seif-interest. This will for peaceful alternatives is further exemplified by at least two working

November 29, 1990
Government Orders
papers that I have, which I can table, that were circulated at the United Nations. From what I understand, neither paper was found worthy of discussion because the United States took exception to them. Yet, both these papers called for dealing with the issue within a peaceful framework that would compliment the sanctions and allow for discussion and movement that could lead, with the right type of encouragement, to a peaceful resolution through diplomacy as the Prime Minister said.
I want to draw to the attention of the House the specific reasons that my colleagues on this side of the House oppose the motion put forth by the government. The Liberal Party has stated on many occasions that it supports all the resolutions that have been put forth to date at the Security Council.
However we cannot support under any circumstances a blank cheque to the government, as is the case in this motion, and I have already mentioned the controversial interpretation by government representatives themselves.
We also cannot support a deadline such as is indicated in the draft resolution to be debated at the United Nations this afternoon. Our party does not want a time line put into that resolution. If that time line were removed, then we certainly would consider it.
We believe that we have not given peace a chance to work. I would like to remind this House that we are not the only ones who feel this way. We are in the company of former U.S. advisers, Schlesinger and Brzezinski, who was here at the Soviet Union conference for three days. We are in the company of the United Nations Association of Canada. We are in the company of 65 per cent of Canadians who believe that the sanctions need more time. But, does this Prime Minister listen to Canadians? Oh, no.
We are also in the company of several Security Council members who are not quite decided on their decision on the vote. From what I understand, an affirmative vote is necessary by 10 of the 15 members and so far four countries are opposed and five others are wavering.
I urge this government to reflect on our country's influence on members of the Security Council. Over the last few days I had my office speak to various people at the UN. We have been told quite explicitly that Canada does not seem to appreciate how crucial our vote will be on the motion; that were we to abstain it would encourage other member countries to vote according to their will, versus voting under pressure from the United States.
The Security Council is not some independent body that exists somewhere in space making decisions. It is made up of individual countries. I truly believe that we would have a consensus at the United Nations, albeit a different one from that which was envisioned. It would not be a move that was unsupportive of the UN, because a majority of members would be in agreement.
These are not only my words. I have had calls from my constituents. I had a call from a daughter whose father is a hostage in Kuwait. His wife and daughter are my constituents. The hostage had to be smuggled into a hospital to have an operation because he had a tumour on his stomach. This is when it hits home. I had calls from other constituents who have asked me to pass on these words, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Prime Minister: "Stop your sabre rattling".
After listening to my constituents on this issue, I would suggest to the government that we take a step back, that we put down our sabres and swords, that we shed this paranoid mentality that is not in keeping with our own, and that we begin by promoting within a peaceful framework action that we would support upon the withdrawal of Iraq forces.
We should begin by talking about timetables for the withdrawal of the multinational forces; about support in setting up a democratic government in Kuwait, because there is not one now; about the convening of an international peace conference, which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has been promoting, to resolve the Palestinian issue.
If all diplomatic initiatives fail and if the longer time for sanctions to work fails, then and only then would we really have credibility in supporting the military option. We have not explored all diplomatic channels. We have not given sanctions time to work. We are not being fair to the Canadians who voted us into this House to go the military option right now.

I will close with these words. The Prime Minister said that the late Lester B. Pearson would be rolling over in his grave if he heard what I said. I ask the Prime Minister if Lester B. Pearson was standing in his place, what option would he choose? Would he recommend the diplomatic channel and the sanction channel, or would he support the sabre-rattling approach of our Prime Minister?
The answer is very clear. The late Lester B. Pearson is with us, smiling. At least some Canadians have not forgotten what he stood for and what the United Nations is standing for; that is, to resolve issues peacefully, without war.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the motion before us, which is asking this House to support the United Nations in its efforts to ensure compliance with Security Council resolution 660 and subsequent resolutions.
I remind the House that we are not here to debate whether the aggression of Saddam Hussein is unacceptable. It is unacceptable. We are not here to debate whether the actions that have been taken either in the past or in the present by Saddam Hussein are insupportable nationally and internationally. They are insupportable.
We are not here to debate whether economic sanctions is a route that we should go. This House has already passed that resolution. This party has already supported that resolution.
We are here and are asked to support a resolution which is basically a blank cheque for war. We are asked to support any resolution, not specific resolutions. It has been decades since Canada has been at war. Instead, we have paid the role of peacekeeper, of mediator, of a bridge between east and west, north and south.
While our record has not always been perfect, our commitment to the principles of dialogue, negotiation and peaceful solutions has served us well in the international community.
The government's motion represents a sharp and historic move away from the traditional role of peacekeeper. It represents a move to military solutions and to participation in war.
Government Orders
My party takes a back seat to no one in our condemnation of Saddam Hussein. My party is not willing to discard the principles which have served this country so well. Canada must look at peaceful options and solutions to a crisis in the Gulf.
Canadians, as the Prime Minister himself has said, are a peaceful people. We cannot and must not move hastily into a war. Therefore my party cannot support the government's motion. I want to cite two major reasons for this. First, by supporting the draft UN resolution, I draw your attention to the words "use all necessary means".
We would be signalling, by supporting this motion, support for the use of military force as a means to resolve the conflict by an artificial deadline, a deadline which I remind the Prime Minister his own Secretary of State for External Affairs said he had some great difficulty with.
This is not the time for Canadians to go against their conscience. It is the time for Canadians to stand up for peace.
My party believes that such an option as proposed by this motion is premature. We are saying, give sanctions a chance. Give diplomacy a chance. Patience and common sense are crucial at this time.
Second, any Canadian participation in the use of military force would not, given the wording of the government's motion, require the involvement and consent of this Parliament. Once again, it would allow closed door, back room, old style decision making. We were asked to give consent to anything that was passed behind these doors, without the Canadians being included in this debate and fully aware of all of the ramifications of the actions which would be taken.

This would be a logical extension of the government's actions last summer, when the Prime Minister, with total disregard for public opinion and the democratic process, decided to send troops to the Persian Gulf without consulting Parliament.
Read the papers!

Only last week, our troops participated in military exercises that went well beyond their mandate as defined by Parliament and well beyond the parameters of the UN resolutions endorsed by this Parliament.

Government Orders

My party believes that Canadians must be consulted. They must be given all of the information and much greater discussion must take place in this House. It must agree on any change in our status in the Persian Gulf.
The government is asking for a blank cheque and we are saying no. We reject this motion. We reject it because it is misguided and because it is wrong.
Let us look at the options with which we are confronted.

The invasion of Kuwait by Saddam Hussein on August 2 and the occupation of that country constitute a flagrant violation of international law. Such action is unacceptable and shocking to all people who believe in freedom.
This contempt for human rights is not an isolated incident. Saddam Hussein does not have a good record on human rights. In fact, he has one of the worst. He even used chemical weapons against his own people. I am sure everyone in this House will agree that Iraq must withdraw from Kuwait.

We have no difference, therefore, on the final goal. The question and the point on which our approaches differ is what is the best response to Hussein's actions? What is the best, most rational and least costly route to achieve our goals? Is it economic sanctions and international isolation, or is it war?
The government suggests that economic sanctions are not working but it gives us no evidence to support that argument. We, on the contrary, have reason to believe that sanctions are working. Several witnesses appearing before the Standing Committee on International Affairs have argued that sanctions are effective. German hostages just released from Iraq tell us that the effects of sanctions are beginning to show. An American admiral has argued that the embargo is working. A former director of the CIA says he believes that the embargo will work.
I remind the House that Iraq relies on imports for over 80 per cent of its basic materials. It is dependent on the sale of oil for 95 per cent of its export earnings. Sanctions are supported world-wide. Iraq is totally isolated. They
are feeling the effects now. Given four, six or eight months, those effects may well be impossible to bear for Saddam Hussein.
How can the government say that sanctions will not work. They can work. What is needed is patience, strength and resolve. We must give sanctions a chance.

I would like to add, Mr. Speaker, that the position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the use of sanctions is highly inconsistent. When he talked about South Africa, the Secretary of State was very much in favour of sanctions. He said they were effective. He argued that we had to be patient. He was sure that if we were prepared to wait, the sanctions would produce results.
So I have a question for the Prime Minister: Why South Africa and not Iraq?

Sanctions and international pressure forced South Africa out of Namibia. The United Nations played a peaceful and meaningful role in restoring independence to that country. Let that example guide us in our new post-cold war era of international relations.
Mr. Speaker, the government argued that we must resort to force because it is the only language Saddam Hussein understands. However, we cannot be absolutely sure that Saddam Hussein is impervious to other arguments if we do not keep conciliation and peace on the agenda. We must be absolutely sure.

Mr. Speaker, we must look at the implications of war. We must consider them directly and head on. Let there be no mistake. The cost of war would be high. Hundreds of thousands of lives may be lost, many of them civilian, and it is clear that Canadian men and women, including those hostages still in Iraq, would be among the casualties. We are talking about another generation of young people, of lives full of promise and potential, ended.
There is a good reason why the rapidly growing anti-war movement in the United States is being led by Vietnam veterans. They know the reality. They have
November 29, 1990

been there. They are saying: "Don't do it again". It is time to listen to them.
No one believes that a war would be short, that a war would be contained just between Iraq and Kuwait. There is a real chance of a war in the Middle East escalating into a conflict which encompasses the entire Middle East. The horrors of chemical weapons, of nuclear weapons, and the use of those in that region is not outside the realm of possibility.
A war in the Gulf will destroy lives, will devastate nations. We must do everything we can to avoid it.
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the House that if the New Democratic Party wanted to wait months for sanctions to work that that is our decision. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is our decision.
Hear, hear.

It is one that we counsel this government to follow because by waiting months we may prevent a war that lasts for years and we may prevent pain that lasts a lifetime.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that voting against this motion does not in any way mean we reject the resolutions adopted by the UN so far. What we reject is the resolution drafted by the United States. I may add, Mr. Speaker, that an increasing number of Americans is against this motion.

What we are saying, Mr. Speaker, to the Canadian government, to the Prime Minister, is that he must go to the United Nations, to the Security Council and ask them to hold the course on sanctions, to let sanctions work and to commit again that Canada will do its fair share to ensure that those economic sanctions are implemented.
Mr. Speaker, the government will surely say that Canada must be tough and we must be strong. I agree. But to be tough sometimes means trying to bring others around to your view than just giving in to theirs.
Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, to be strong means to be patient and to show resolve. To be strong means searching until exhaustion for peaceful solutions. To be strong means seeking dialogue when others seek destruction.
Government Orders
Our amendment to the government's motion underlines the view that the Canadian government must speak for Canadians by demonstrating a strong commitment to peace. In every decision it makes in this crisis it must consult the people of Canada or it will not be supported by the people of Canada.
It has been said that the road to war is a wide one and the path to peace is often narrow and difficult to find. Let us offer the world some hope. Let Canada be a voice of calm. Let Canada be a voice of reason. Let Canada be a voice for peace.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment. With regard to the issue of war, when it comes down to the reconciliation of some rather major decisions that have to be made, it is never easy, there is never a right answer and no one in his or her right mind goes against the idea of peace. Having said that, on October 23 a motion was put to this House:
That this House condemn the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq and, encouraged by the unprecedented international consensus demanding the immediate and unconditional withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait and the full restoration of the legitimate government of Kuwait, affirm unequivocally its support for Canada's actions in the Security Council-
Having embodied here the condemnation of Iraq for the invasion of Kuwait, I would like to know why the New Democratic Party did not support the condemnation of Iraq by voting for this particular motion on October 23, 1990.
I would like the Leader of the New Democratic Party to give us her reconciliation on this whole motion. Indeed, it was a difficult one even for our party. We put forward a motion and by changing some of the wording, we accepted it because the discussion of any kind of peace initiative or any kind of discussion about war is a very serious and difficult one for any party. I ask the hon. member to please respond.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Western Arctic for her comments. As a member from the north, I share the north with the hon. member for Western Arctic, and I think we have some understanding about the threats of living very close to a superpower, as we do in the north. I believe the member for Western Arctic pointed that out in her own comments.

Government Orders
I appreciate her comments, in terms of the motion that she refers to. We have always been unequivocal in condemning the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq. Once again, the government brought forth motions to this House that were opened-ended and that allowed for going beyond the specifics. That is what this government wants again with this motion before us today. One would not even buy a house without knowing what is in it, but this government wants to agree to any kind of resolution, no matter what it is, no matter what is proposed, if it is in the United Nations.
I would have thought a party which prides itself on business would want to make sure that it was being full and open with this House and with the Canadian public about what it is asking the public to agree to and what it is asking this House of Commons to agree to. We do not need open-ended resolutions; we need this government to stand up in front of the public of Canada, to be accountable for its actions, and to tell us what evidence it has that economic sanctions are not working because it has never once in this House been able to tell anyone what evidence it has that economic sanctions are not working.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest and with care to the comments of the Leader of the New Democratic Party. This is indeed a difficult debate for all parliamentarians. It is a difficult debate for Canadians and people all over the world who love peace, strive for peace, and want to see a world where we do not have madmen like Saddam Hussein who take over countries, trample on people's sovereign rights, their human rights, maim, kill, and have no respect for international law. It is a very complex issue and I know that the resolution that is before us today, the one from the government, obviously is too open-ended. It is flawed, but that is typical of the type of resolutions that this government always puts forward on serious matters .The government did the same thing on the resolution about sending troops over to the Persian Gulf. It cannot seem to get it right.
I want to ask the Leader of the New Democratic Party, what is the position of her party. I have looked at the proposed amendment that has been put forward. It talks about allowing sanctions to work. Under what circumstances and what conditions would her party be able to
support other efforts, other than sanctions? I am talking about the possible use of force. Does she foresee any circumstances where the possible use of force would be something that should be considered and would be supported by her party?

Mr. Speaker, clearly we do not know what is going to happen in the future. The first step we have to take is to make sure that we have done everything. I think that the Liberal Party is in agreement, that we cannot accept an open-ended resolution until we have shown that everything else has been done before we take an offensive action. I think we should be clear here that what is being discussed in the Middle East is not a defensive action by the United States, Canada and other countries, but an offensive action which can lead to disastrous consequences.
Therefore, we are saying very clearly that we need to allow time for economic sanctions to work. It is not just the New Democratic Party that has said this. Gwynne Dyer, when he gave his testimony before the international affairs committee, other experts, other military analysts have said that it takes six months to a year before we can really see whether the economic sanctions are working. We must do that. We must give those sanctions a chance.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the member is right in the sense that the sanctions are the way to go, in the sense that time must be given to see that sanctions work. What we are facing in real terms is whether or not it is appropriate to send a message ultimately to somebody who has committed an act of aggression, a country that has committed an act of aggression against another country, that we are not prepared to wait forever.
The passage of a UN resolution that provides power to an international force does not mean that the power gets executed in the next two minutes, or the next five minutes, or the next five days, or even the next five months. However, there is a message in it.
Surely, the New Democratic Party agrees with the message that in no way, at no time, can the country of Iraq be rewarded for having committed the act of aggression. Surely, we as a world community with all of our experience that tracks back to the League of Nations and the United Nations have to say that we prefer a world community for the future, for our children and our grandchildren, where the world operates together under

United Nations sanction and we as a world community prefer to say to any country we will not tolerate aggression and if pushed to the wall, we are willing to back up our resolutions with whatever force has to be there. We cannot simply deal in world terms with rhetoric.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do not know whether there was a question but if the hon. member for Yukon would like to rebut.

Mr. Speaker, if economic sanctions were not a strong message, why did this government propose them? Economic sanctions are a strong message. This government and our own party have been proposing for years that economic sanctions in South Africa are a strong message.
Economic sanctions are a strong message.
We do not support aggression, but we believe we have to take all steps before we do anything else. I remind the hon. member that this resolution would give agreement to any resolution that might be made, without specifying what would be in that resolution. That is unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes that remain, I am pleased to have an opportunity to enter into this debate.
All of us recently experienced the Remembrance Day ceremonies. I know, as I have been a member in this House now for a little over 10 years, the Remembrance Day ceremonies are always a special time of tribute to our veterans, to those Canadians who did serve to protect our country and our interests, and to those who gave up their lives in that last war.
The first unique thing about this ceremony this year as I was attending those Remembrance Day services is that it was conducted by a young woman who was the minister but who was also a member of Canada's reserves.
In that audience were several other young people who were members of the reserves of the Canadian Armed Forces. What was unique about this particular service was that these young people, even though we were there remembering past wars and victims, I was there with young people who may well be called upon by their
Government Orders
country to serve in an action that all of us were looking at each night on our television screens.
What intrigued me was to hear the attitude of these young people, the concerns for their families and country, and about the implications of what may well happen in that part of the world. It did add, I thought, a very unique dimension and a very touching dimension to those services this last Remembrance Day.
The other comment that I want to mention is that I have always enjoyed reading novels of a historical nature. One of the things that seems to come to mind when we look at history is, of course, that perspective of hindsight that somehow takes war and glamourizes it. It somehow separates it from us in a certain way. We look at the spectacular and successful actions-all of the events that go on in a war-but we are left with a sense of distance.
Yet, today we find ourselves in a very unique position in that with the television communications, particularly, and with our print media, what can happen so many miles away from us can have an instantaneous impact on our nation.
Somebody living in the community of Peace River will feel a very significant effect.

Mr. Speaker, just on a brief point of order, I feel that for those of us in the House here-in fact, Canadians across the country watching this-it looks like a replay of the Grey Cup and watching the CFL time killers in action.

Mr. Speaker, our mail presently goes to the Persian Gulf via a depot in Halifax. In order to send mail to that depot, Canadian people have to pay the cost of the mail.
I have spoken to the Minister of National Defence and written to the minister in charge of the Post Office to see if during the Christmas season parcels, care packages, presents, letters and cards could not be sent free of charge to the depot in Halifax.
This is one way for Canada to say "Thank you" to the men and women who serve in the Gulf and who are there through our government's policies, perhaps not by choice, and in very dangerous times.
I call on the minister in charge of Canada Post to ask Canada Post to stop putting profits before service in this particular area and allow the mail in Canada to go free of charge to Halifax and on to the Gulf during the next month. In fact, it should go free all the time to our men and women who are serving in the Gulf.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise in the House today to inform my colleagues of the outstanding achievement of a company which employs many people in my constituency.
On October 31, 1990 one of the largest employers in my riding, Northern Telecom Canada Limited of Bramalea, Ontario was honoured with a Gold 1990 Canada Award for Business Excellence in the category of outstanding quality.
I can say without reservation that Northern Telecom is an impressive operation, conscious of producing an outstanding product, while maintaining an excellent working environment for its employees. With this winning combination, I am confident that Northern Telecom Canada Limited will continue to be successful and will remain a respected member of the community of Bramalea. Again, congratulations Northern Telecom.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday in this House the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was asked about the future of the core area initiative in Winnipeg. He replied that he would do what was best for Winnipeg.
We found out subsequently that best means eliminating the core area initiative, cutting back on projects in the inner city and leaving the 100,000 people who live there in need of federal moneys but without any support.

It is hard to believe that now, at the last moment, he has finally discovered that he does not like North Portage, that he does not like the Forks, he does not like the core, but somehow up until this time he could not find a way of speaking about it.
The minister said that he needs a public evaluation before he continues. If he needs a public evaluation, he should have thought about it months ago because people in Winnipeg have been asking for the renewal for many weeks now. Instead, the minister should commit himself in Winnipeg to the renewal of the core and to a commitment to improve the conditions of Winnipeg's inner city.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the government an editorial which appeared yesterday in the Winnipeg Free Press. The editorial correctly points out the need for the federal government to maintain national health care standards. The editorial also points out that for the last 10 years Liberal and Tory governments have gradually reduced the federal share of funding for Canada's health care system.
The reduction started when the Liberal's new leader was Minister of Finance. He started the erosion of our health care system and the Conservatives were only too eager to follow his lead.
Mr. Speaker, it is because of the vision of Tommy Douglas that Canada has one of the best health care systems anywhere. I find it disgraceful that the federal Conservatives and Liberals still yearn for an American style system. It is obvious that Canada's health care system is not safe under either the Conservatives or the Liberals.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's veterans are supporting our armed forces in the Gulf in a very heart-warming way. In particular, I am
talking about members of the Alberta command of the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada.
Recently Command President Mr. Cecil Burke handed over a cheque for $120,000 to the Base Commander, Canadian Forces Base, Edmonton. The money will be used to buy televisions, video-cassette recorders and satellite dish antennae for the enjoyment of our forces personnel in the Gulf.
Mr. Burke said: "Most of us have an idea of what they are going through over there". I congratulate members of Canada's oldest veterans organization for rallying round those whose turn it is now to wear the uniform of Canada in a far-away land.


TRIBUTE TO JEAN-FRAN^OIS BOUCHARD

Mr. Speaker, allow me to pay tribute to an eight-year-old boy called Jean-Frangois Bouchard. He is the son of Mr. and Mrs. Jean-Paul Bouchard of my riding. The reason for this tribute is the following. On October 28, Jean-Frangois took part in a Halloween skating event. Everyone had a great time until Jean-Frangois fell and had most of one finger cut off. The strength, courage and, let us say the word, bravery displayed by this young boy were impressive. This is why I wanted to draw special attention to it.
Mr. Speaker, small children have a way of teaching us adults singular lessons of logic and positive thinking. This young boy has quite a future ahead of him. I am sure of that.

Mr. Speaker, the tax reform implemented in 1988 is having positive results. The 1988 tax statistics indicate that low-income Canadians do benefit from the reform. That same year, the average after tax income rose by 8.6 per cent. The number of Canadians over age 65 who do not pay any tax has increased by more than 40 per cent and now stands at 290,000.
The income tax reform has made the system more progressive and more equitable. The sales tax reform is an additional stage in that process. High-income Canadians will be paying a larger share of their income
November 29, 1990

through the sales tax, whereas families with an income of $30,000 or less will be better off than they are now.
All things considered, the tax reform combined with other important measures taken by the government to boost the Canadian economy will make the tax system more equitable, improve competitiveness and create more jobs.
