Mr. Speaker, the environment is everyone's concern but it is of special concern to our next generation.
Grade six students at Westmount School in Moose Jaw have written to advise me that they have studied the effects of acid rain. One student writes: "We have discovered that acid rain causes fish, plants and animals to die, lakes to be ruined and animal reproduction difficulties".
Another writes: "It is very important to stop acid rain because Canadian lakes are very sensitive to acid rain and we share 25 per cent of the world's fresh water supply".
The government should heed the pleas of these students. They are speaking on behalf of students right across the country. The government should ensure that a national acid rain program which places a cap on emissions and sets national standards will be included in the upcoming Green Plan.
Certainly the fact that the three western provinces and the two territories are not now included in any plan leaves over one-half of Canada's environment unprotected.
I say well done to the students at Westmount School. Let us all hope that the government is listening.

subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext: Next week, Mr. Speaker, Canada will play an important role in the GATT negotiations in Brussels. It was Prime Minister Mulroney who, at the outset of this critical round four years ago, insisted that agriculture be put on the negotiation agenda. Last year the industrialized nations paid out something like $250 billion in farm subsidies, yet a good many agricultural producers throughout the world are still hard-pressed, except perhaps in Europe where the EEC is thwarting progress. The international agricultural trade system does not work, and that spells disaster for some Canadian farmers. We and our agricultural producers simply cannot accept a failure next week, and certainly not the status quo.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice visited Winnipeg last weekend and commented on the David Milgaard case.

November 29, 1990
Milgaard has spent more than 20 years in prison for murder, but there is serious doubt that he committed the crime. For many months we have pressed the justice minister to make a decision in the case. On Winnipeg television she said: "In the third week in September I was advised the file was ready for me but that they," being department officials, "had received communication from Milgaard's counsel that he wished to make more argument".
Where does the justice minister get this stuff? She is dead wrong. Milgaard's counsel, David Asper, said in the same broadcast: "We completed our submission during the summer". By the way, that was confirmed in a September 10 letter from Asper to the Department of Justice.
The minister had better get a grip on her department. Someone is feeding her a line. It puts justice under a cloud and makes her look like a fool.

In his movie entitled "Jesus of Montreal", Mr. Speaker, Denys Ar-cand offers a satire of the advertising industry and the way this industry exploits the physical attributes of women to sell their wares. Unfortunately, as any other good satire, Denys Arcand's is a fairly accurate reflection of the truth.
Mr. Speaker, who among us has not noticed the degrading representation of women by our major advertising agencies and their customers? Is it necessary to use a woman's body to sell beer or chewing gum? All advertising agencies are well aware that by trying to sell their wares that way, they are selling sex. I suggest this is an unhealthy if not dangerous attitude to cultivate in a society where violence against women is definitely on the rise.

Mr. Speaker, six years ago the government amended the Canada and Quebec pension plans to bring them into line with the
equality provisions in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The government imposed equality at the same time on all private sector pension plans it regulates, yet it has failed to eliminate inequities and injustices in the pension plans for its own employees.
Survivors of Public Service pensions still get only a 50 per cent pension, compared to the 60 per cent the government imposes on other funds. Part-time employees are left out of the pension plan, contributing further to the poverty of women.
The government is withholding from Public Service employees changes that are their right under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
It is holding these changes in reserve to sugar coat the bitter bill it plans to deliver when it deindexes the pensions Public Service employees have paid for over many years.
When will the government treat its own employees with the same pension equality it imposes on all other employers?

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my most heartfelt appreciation and gratitude to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and its responsible minister, Hon. Allan Redway, for the financial support my constituents of La Prairie, on the south shore of Montreal, have received from the corporation which, through its grants, has made it possible since my election in 1984 to build approximately 200 low-rental housing units for senior citizens.
Mr. Speaker, as a result of an agreement on social housing, reached in 1986 by the Quebec government and the Government of Canada I will have the honour to officially open on December 1 the Memoir de Brossard, a complex of 61 low-rental housing units for senior citizens.
This opening is the concrete result of the joint efforts of the CMHC, the Quebec Housing Corporation, the Brossard Municipal Housing Bureau and myself to provide our senior citizens with decent housing.
November 29, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I thank the CMHC and my minister for their tremendous contributions.

Mr. Speaker, just last week this government fed Canadians the line that it needed money to pay for its action in the Gulf. Yet every Canadian knows that its greatest overspending costs were due to its bad judgment in estimating the costs of its high interest rate policies and bringing in the GST, all policies for which Canadian taxpayers have to pay.
Now after cutting funding for programs for people, Finance Minister Michael Wilson is so insensitive that he spent $250,000 of Canadian taxpayers' money to peddle government propaganda to the business community. The minister's video titled, "Where Do Your Taxpayer Dollars Go?", should really have been called "Thx Lies and Videotape".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the current environmental debate, there is one major stakeholder whose efforts to apply the principles of sustainable development often go unnoticed.
Industry is concerned about sustainable development and the environmental challenge before us. In particular today, I wish to commend the Canadian mining industry.
It is a little known fact that Canadians are leading the way in sustainable mining. Under the leadership of the Mining Association of Canada, our mining sector has produced for itself a Guide for Environmental Practice.
Canadian mining companies are committed to sound environmental practices at home and abroad. The mining sector is committed to responsible product stewardship. The mining community is very aware of environmental problems and is eager to participate in vital debate begun with the work of the Brundtland report.
Oral Questions
As a major stakeholder, a provider of wealth for our country, the Canadian mining sector has a valuable contribution to make for environmentally sustainable economic development.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and is about Canada's involvement in the crisis in the Persian Gulf. On Monday, the Minister for International Trade, speaking on behalf of the government about the sanctions against Iraq said in this House:
-the Secretary of State for External Affairs is quite prepared to make available to the House, or to the Standing Committee on External Affairs, the full information on how effective the sanctions policy appears to be.
Yesterday, when speaking in this House, the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave no such information and no such evidence. All he did was say, in effect, that the sanctions were not working and today in the House the Prime Minister said the same thing.
Will the Prime Minister give us the evidence promised by the Minister for International Tirade that the sanctions are not working? This evidence is important because it affects how Canadians look at the risk some Canadians are under in the Persian Gulf. Why will the Prime Minister not give us the evidence promised on behalf of this government? Why will he not give us that evidence today?

Mr. Speaker, first let me just correct a misstatement by my hon. friend in regard to my statement this morning in the House. What I said was: "While the UN sanctions are undoubtedly being felt by the Iraqi and Kuwaiti people, we have found no wide-spread confidence that they are sufficient to bring about the desired result to namely persuade President Hussein to withdraw his forces from Kuwait". I think that is an important distinction that my hon. friend would want to bear in mind.
As to any information that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have available regarding the results of the sanction policy, I am sure that, immediately

November 29, 1990
Oral Questions
upon his return from New York, he would be happy to provide this to my hon. friend.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the time to provide that evidence was during the debate which has just concluded. Canadians will want to know why the government did not have enough confidence in its own policy to provide that evidence before now. Canadians need that evidence before the vote is taken in the United Nations on the resolution in question.
Yesterday, the immediate past chairman of the United States Joint Chiefs of Staff, Admiral William Crowe, said in testimony before a United States Senate committee, when speaking about the sanctions against Iraq and how they are working: "I counsel patience, war is not neat, it is not tidy, it is a mess". That is what Admiral Crowe said.
Is it possible that the reason the government has not given us the evidence it claims it has about how the sanctions are working is because it knows all the evidence is of the kind provided by Admiral Crowe, that the sanctions are working and they need more time to work and the time has not yet arrived, nor is it near, for offensive action? Is that not the fact?

Mr. Speaker, it really is quite a shameful suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition, to say nothing of the fact that I find passing strange the manner in which some days the Liberal Party loves the Americans and most days, they do not. When they find an American who says something with which they agree, they are actively quoting him.
The issue before the House is the issue we addressed this morning, support for the United Nations.
We support the United Nations.

My friend says "We support the United Nations". The United Nations has passed 10 resolutions requesting that they withdraw from Kuwait. This will be the eleventh resolution for which the United Nations is seeking support.
Mr. Pearson said in 1945: "Never again should an aggressor be permitted to strike down one nation after another before the peace loving nations of the world organize and take concerted action against it." The
United Nations is seeking the support of peace-loving nations to take concerted action against it, and Canada is going to provide that support.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the Prime Minister says that he is a great supporter of the United Nations, and so is his government. These words are strange in light of the fact that a few days ago the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that they were ready to get involved in offensive action against Iraq unilaterally whether the UN approved it or not. Those are not the words of somebody who puts his primary faith in the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, Conservative Senator Gerald Beaudoin, the constitutional expert, said that the government would not have to call back Parliament if it were to decide in favour of armed intervention against Iraq. Mr. Speaker, this statement contradicts a government motion adopted by this House on October 23.
I therefore want to ask the Prime Minister: Will he repudiate today the statements made by Senator Beaudoin and will he announce his intention to respect his commitment to call back Parliament before Canadian troops are involved in a military offensive in the Persian Gulf?

Mr. Speaker, I did not read the senator's statement, but my hon. friend can hardly expect me to start commenting on all the statements being made in the Senate, because we would be here for quite some time. As for the second part of his question, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself have, on various occasions, dealt with this point satisfactorily. However, the Leader of the Opposition-inadvertently, I expect-misquoted what I said. In fact, he said, suggesting that he was quoting me verbatim:

-"the Prime Minister said that we are ready to get involved to get in an offensive action against Iraq unilaterally whether the United Nations approved or not". I never made any such statement.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and concerns the government's non-tabling of requested sanctions documentation.

The Prime Minister's answers to the hon. House leader's questions a few moments ago are ringing in my ears. They echo almost exactly the answer we got to the same question in this House on Monday of this week when the Minister for International Trade responded: "I am quite sure that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is quite prepared to make available to the House the full information on the effect of sanctions policies". Canadians accept an embargo against Iraq, but not an embargo against providing Canadians vital information concerning sanctions. We requested information. We did not get it.
Why has the government refused to provide this vital information concerning sanctions against Iraq?

Mr. Speaker, the government is not refusing to provide information. I have already indicated to my hon. friend that when the question was asked, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is responsible for this, was in Jordan meeting with King Hussein and in Israel meeting with Prime Minister Shamir. He then flew back, spoke at a meeting here in Ottawa, spoke in the House, and is now speaking before the Security Council at the United Nations.
I indicated to my hon. friend that when the information is made available to me, presumably immediately upon my right hon. friend's return, we will be happy to provide my hon. friend with all of the information that we have.
The issue before the House yesterday, today and tomorrow in respect of Iraq is going to be whether this party, this government and this House supports the United Nations in what it is seeking to do. We will provide full support, as we will provide my hon. friend with all of the information available to us.
We seek peace in the region, but peace in the region will come through firm and unwavering support for the resolutions of the UN Security Council.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also to the Prime Minister. Canada has supported and this party has supported the imposition of UN sanctions against Iraq as an effective method of forcing Iraq out of Kuwait. Other
Oral Questions
nations, such as Colombia, have proposed other peacemaking solutions to the Middle East crisis to the UN Security Council. What evidence can the government give us today that Canada has pursued other peaceful resolutions to the Middle East crisis prior to supporting the UN resolution before the Security Council today?

Mr. Speaker, I can tell my hon. friend that in co-operation with a number of other nations, Canada has been working privately, and I hope with some effect, to assist in what we hope will be a peaceful resolution of this very important matter. This has been done at the United Nations directly with the Secretary General. It has been done through a number of our important alliances and in other initiatives around the world. We hope that will contribute in a beneficial way.

Mr. Speaker, today a resolution was passed in this House, not supported by this party, which basically gave blanket support to any resolution that the United Nations might pass, because it is not clear what will be contained in subsequent UN resolutions. It simply says the Security Council resolution and all subsequent relevant resolutions, but no specifics.
Given the fact that there are no specifics attached to what resolutions this government has just supported, if the United States were to decide to invade Iraq after January 15, which is the deadline given in the UN resolution, does this government resolution mean today that the Prime Minister has given George Bush his approval and that he can have Canadian support for an attack of Iraq after January 15?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend seriously would not want me to answer that kind of canard. I wonder why she devised the hypothetical question with Mr. Bush in mind. Perhaps she missed the statement by Soviet President Gorbachev this week who delivered an ultimatum to Iraq warning it to withdraw from Kuwait or face the worst consequences. Gorbachev is reported to have told the Iraqi Foreign Minister, Mr. Aziz: "If Iraq really wanted a settlement in the entire region and is interested in avoiding the worst, it must now openly pull out of Kuwait and release hostages".

Oral Questions
President Gorbachev concluded: "The President of Iraq must weigh everything once more. The fate of Iraq is in the hands of its leaders, and time is expiring."
President Gorbachev is expressing a pretty universally held sentiment, with the possible exception of a few people in the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister then: What did we vote on this morning?
What does he mean by the kind of sanctions that will be effective January 15? I ask the Prime Minister again: In this UN resolution, what is his understanding of exactly what will occur after January 15 if Saddam Hussein has not withdrawn from Kuwait by that time?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Chair is in some difficulty. That is a very hypothetical question. Within the rules, it is out of order.
I would ask the hon. member to perhaps rephrase her question.

Mr. Speaker, we were asked to vote this morning on a resolution that said in effect that we would support any resolution, not specified, that the United Nations would pass.
What does the Prime Minister anticipate those other resolutions would be?

Mr. Speaker, the motion refers to the resolution that is being debated at the United Nations today. That is the position.
That is why President Gorbachev indicated publicly in Paris that it was imperative that the United Nations receive unanimous support, if at all possible, for the resolution that was going to be voted today, because he did not want the United Nations to go the route of the League of Nations, which disintegrated and was unable to provide the strong international leadership that the world needs.
The United Nations asked for Canada's support in the defence of universal rights. That was granted today by the Government of Canada, and I hope eventually by members of my hon. friend's party.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is well aware of what the UN resolution says and, I assume, what his own resolution says.
It asks this House to give a blank cheque to vote for any resolution that the UN might give.
I have a question on another very serious subject related to the issue in the Middle East.

Everyone is this country is delighted that seven Canadian hostages were able to leave Iraq, but we are concerned about the fate of the remaining hostages. I want to ask the Prime Minister to tell the House what his government intends to do to ensure that the remaining Canadian hostages will also be able to go home.

Mr. Speaker, in my comments this morning I pointed out that one of the cornerstones of the government's foreign policy in this area was freeing the hostages. The government has embarked on a series of initiatives and is working very hard to help the hostages and their families.
It is also important to point out that President Gorbachev asked Foreign Minister Aziz in Moscow about 48 hours ago to proceed immediately. He asked Iraq to proceed immediately with the release of all hostages held in Iraq.

My question is directed to the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday, the Government of Quebec approved a federal-provincial agreement on impact studies for the Great Whale project. The Quebec environment minister said very clearly that the agreement did not include infrastructures. On October 18, in reply to a question here in the House, the federal environment minister said, and I quote: "With my Quebec counterpart we are having a discussion of the terms of reference which will cover the infrastructures". This is my question: Who is telling the truth?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to make it very clear to this House that there is in fact no agreement between the Government of Quebec and the
November 29, 1990

Government of Canada on this issue. There is a response by the Government of Quebec to a proposal made by the Government of Canada on November 20.
I think it is perfectly reasonable, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member would not ask us to respond to that counter-proposal until the Minister of the Environment, who is meeting in Victoria with his provincial counterparts, meeting by the way to discuss very important issues, including consulting with them on the green plan, has an opportunity to examine the document and to respond at the appropriate time.
Because he asked a question before, I want to assure him, as the Minister of the Environment has done on numerous occasions, that there will be an environmental assessment of both the infrastructure and the project itself and that this environmental assessment will be a public process.

What a tangled web we weave. I have a document dated July 6 which sets out the principles of an agreement reached between the two Ministers of the Environment. That agreement specifically excludes the infrastructures. The agreement is in French:

"Quebec and Canada have agreed to submit the Great Whale complex to an environmental assessment. For the purposes of this joint assessment, the complex excludes access infrastructures."

Does the government deny that the agreement sent from Quebec last night contains the exclusion that I have just cited? Does the government deny that the agreement was arrived at by the federal Minister of the Environment at the end of June? Does the government deny that that clause is in complete contradiction of the principles that the minister has stated? Does the government deny that the minister's public statements are simply not borne out by his private action?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member, who I believe is a member of the legal profession, must surely understand that there is a very major distinction between the word "agreement" which he chooses to use-and I
Oral Questions
may say he probably does so for his own political advantage-and the question of a proposal. There have been a series of proposals and counter-proposals back and forth between the two governments. What we have today is a response by the Government of Quebec to the latest proposal which we put on the table on November 20. We will be responding at the appropriate time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and concerns the Spicer commission. It seems the Prime Minister does not intend to fill the seat left vacant by Mrs. Therese Paquet-Sevigny, thus diminishing the contribution of women and francophones to the future of this country.
Mr. Speaker, we are sorry to hear the Prime Minister did not appoint someone else, and that I want to ask him whether he is prepared to acknowledge that the Commission is merely a smoke-screen and that he has failed miserably in his task to keep this country together and united.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that my hon. friend, who usually shows a special interest in important questions concerning national unity, should make such a suggestion.
First of all, regarding the claim that I had decided not to proceed with a new appointment, I simply want to say to my hon. friend that I am having consultations on the membership of the commission. We have suffered a slight setback. Why? Because an exceptional woman, who was posted at the United Nations, agreed to sit on the Commission and subsequently was told that her acceptance might have an impact on administrative decisions at the UN. In the circumstances, she had to withdraw. There is nothing dishonourable about that. There is no negative reflection, either on her or the government. The seats on the commission will be filled, and I am sure the Spicer commission will continue its work and will end up gathering tremendous support for Canada.

November 29, 1990
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Spicer commission, from what reports we get from the press, has no work mandate. It has no work plan. Its members are part time. The Prime Minister tells us he is hesitating to name an additional or additional members to that commission.
Given the importance of this commission to the future of this country, is the Prime Minister prepared today to tell this House that he will name a replacement for the person that left the commission, Madam Paquet-Sevig-ny? Will he show us today by his efforts that he will do everything to make a success of this commission and appoint people to the commission who will be full time and will work in the interests of Canadians and the future of the country?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why my hon. friend has such little faith in the capacity of these people to do very good job for Canada. I fail to understand as well why he is so negative in regard to the manner in which the commission has begun its work.
It took some four months before the composition of Quebec's Belanger-Campeau commission was completed. Indeed, the assembly had to be reconvened to provide for the admission of additional members.
Why would my hon. friend be alarmed at the fact that one member of the Spicer Commission had to resign for reasons that I have explained and conclude therefrom that it will not be effective?
I tell my hon. friend that the Spicer commission will make an effective and I believe durable contribution to the well-being of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
Yesterday Canada's environment took a serious backroom beating from Premier Bourassa and the Quebec Liberals. Their unilateral decision to proceed with the $600 million infrastructure of the Great Whale project is both a threat and an insult.
Since this is part of the largest industrial project ever conceived in the history of North America, will the Prime Minister demonstrate that he believes what he said about the environment when he spoke before the United Nations and assure this House that there will be no federal permits or authorization given on the infrastructure until the entire project has been given a full public environmental assessment and review? Yes or no?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I explained just a moment ago to my hon. friend opposite, the Government of Quebec has made a proposal to the Government of Canada which will certainly be considered by the Minister of the Environment, as the hon. member would wish, on his return from these very important meetings in Victoria.
With respect specifically to the question of infrastructure and the question of environmental assessments, I think there are two or three questions which have been asked by the Canadian public and I think they should be answered.
One of these questions is: Will there be a full environmental assessment in which the federal government will participate on both the question of the infrastructure and the question of the project? And the answer to that is yes.
The second question which I think has been asked is whether or not the federal government will issue any permits to those areas which fall into its jurisdiction with respect to the infrastructure until the EARP process has been applied. And the answer to that question is no.

My supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, is again for the Prime Minister.
The Great Whale project has been on the drawing boards since the 1970s. There have been years of opportunity to evaluate Quebec Hydro's secret environmental impact studies publicly.
Would the Prime Minister confirm the simple fact that there has been a political deal, a roll of the dice deal, made between his office, himself and Premier Bourassa to cover up the truly horrific impacts of this project which stands to be an ecological Auschwitz?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not so certain that question is worthy of an answer, but the answer is a simple no.
November 29, 1990

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue.
Since the Government of Quebec has now taken the lead and cancelled its value added tax on books, and since the Minister of National Revenue indicated as recently as yesterday that he would cancel this goods and services tax on books in all probability after it becomes law, if it does come into law, will he today take Quebec's excellent lead and will he, in International Literacy Year, cancel the goods and services tax on all books and learning materials now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should get his facts straight before putting a question of that nature.
Yesterday I made several comments to the Canadian Thx Foundation. When asked about the Quebec situation on books, I said: "We can't start fiddling around with the legislation. It would send out a confusing message. In other words, there will be no changes in the legislation before it is passed".
I went on to say what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance had said in the past, that once the legislation is implemented we will monitor its effects on the economy, on society, and on specific sectors, and could possibly in future make adjustments. But there will be no adjustments prior to January 1, and the tax will be implemented.

Mr. Speaker, we will let Canadians decide who has his facts straight.

My supplementay is directed to the Prime Minister. Tkxing books and other learning materials amounts to encouraging illiteracy. The 5 to 7 million illiterate Canadians who cost in excess of $10 billion a year to the treasury are often among our poorest fellow citizens. What does the Prime Minister intend to do to help these people learn to read and get them out of this vicious circle of poverty?

Mr. Speaker, this government is aware of the importance of cultural industries and cultural sectors as a whole,
Oral Questions
whether related to publishing, cinema, sound recording or theatre. In most sectors the government has established programs to enable the cultural community to progress to the benefit of all Canadians, and we are pursuing our efforts, Mr. Speaker, including in the publishing field.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The minister has said that he had to cut health care research to reduce the deficit. Canadians do not accept that. The minister will never convince Canadians that he had no option.
Would the Minister of National Health and Welfare explain to Canadians why he chose-and this is the point-to single out health care research for such harsh treatment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us take a look at the harsh treatment that is referred to by the hon. member. Since this government came to office, displacing the old Liberal government and its record on research in Canada, NHRDP has increased by some 55 per cent, some $10 million.
In his own province of Quebec, since the Liberals were thrown out, NHRDP grants went from $4,769 million to $7,696 million in the first 11 months of this year.
That is a record on research which speaks for itself. The hon. member can talk about research. This government has funded it.
Hear, hear.

That is not the question, Mr. Speaker. We never said he cut 100 per cent of the program. Indeed the minister himself confirmed that he did cut this program. So I am asking him today why he chose to cut the health care research program, and will he agree to re-instate the full budget for that research program?

November 29, 1990
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me be a bit more specific even about the hon. member's riding. He will be aware of the fact that on October 17,1 wrote to the hon. member to inform him that so far this year $2.9 million had been put into his own constituency by NHRDP.
We can contrast this government's record in his constituency with his vote on Bill C-22, where the position of the Liberal Party was to block research in dealing with the whole area of medicine. Its record has been one of disgrace.
I believe that at any fair comparison between the record of the Liberals on medical research and the record of this government, it will show that while they talk about it they talk a good fight, but they oppose it when it comes to voting.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
I just want to take him back to the answer he gave to a question by my leader. As I heard him and as I think the House heard him, he said that the government's view of the motion which was passed this morning was that, in terms of subsequent resolutions to today, the only UN resolution that was covered was the resolution which will be coming before the Security Council today. That is what he said. That was ably assisted, I may say, by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Will the Prime Minister therefore agree that the government has no House approval for the commitment of Canadian forces to any offensive action against Iraq?

Mr. Speaker, the answer that I gave to the Leader of the NDP is the policy of the government in regard to the question that was raised by her.
With regard to the broader question, which was the subject of debate this morning, I refer my hon. friend to
a statement that he made in the House on October 25, when he said: "The NDP position is that until all has failed, the United Nations must get the complete unqualified support of this government, this Parliament, and this country".
That is what the United Nations got this morning, and the NDP was not there.

Mr. Speaker, with the greatest of respect, that is exactly why the Prime Minister's approval rating is where it is in the country today.
I asked him a very straightforward question. He could have clarified the understanding that his government got. Let me try once more in a slightly different way.
Will the Prime Minister make a commitment today to this House and to the country that before his government commits Canadian forces to offensive action against Iraq, he will come back to this House and seek its approval?

Mr. Speaker, I answered that question in response, I think, to a question from the Leader of the Liberal Party yesterday or the day before yesterday.
I indicated that we had come to the House on September 24 or September 25, for a full debate, that we came to the House yesterday and today for a full debate, and that at any time circumstances warranted we would, of course, come before the House of Commons for a full debate.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations is not in this House, I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister.
Since we now know from press that the Leader of the Liberal Party is going to appear before the Belanger-Campeau commission-and perhaps I appreciate the fact that because the Prime Minister is Prime Minister he would not want to appear before the Belanger-Cam-peau commission-does the Prime Minister or the government intend to have the so-called Quebec lieutenant or someone else representing the federal government
November 29, 1990

appear before this commission to give the federal message to that commission?

Mr. Speaker, I understand that indeed there are press reports to the effect the Leader of the Liberal Party is planning an appearance before the provincial commission.

The House resumed from Tbesday, November 27, consideration of Bill C-40, an act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and Motion No. 17 of Mr. Waddell (p. 15801); and Motion No. 30 of Mrs. Finestone (p. 15801).

Mr. Speaker, it is my distinct pleasure to speak today to Bill C-40, an act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication, as reported with amendments from a legislative committee.
Although this bill encompasses several positive steps, it needs further revision. The motion before us today addresses one of the fundamental flaws of this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, as you have indicated, we are resuming debate on motions which include the excellent motion of the hon. member for Mount Royal which is before us for
discussion. The motion reflects the deep dissatisfaction within the substance of Bill C-40. This bill drops the CBC's 1968 mandated role to foster Canadian national unity. Specifically it reads:
- to contribute to the development of national unity and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity.
For the first time in Canadian broadcasting history, the national role of the CBC was reaffirmed and legally bound to resist threats to unity. I have read the rationale for removing this fundamental clause but I simply cannot agree with it.
I was all the more concerned when the independent member for Shefford, Quebec, spoke to this motion on Tbesday. I guess the Bloc Quebecois separatist position matches quite well with its desire to see the CBC robbed of its longstanding mandate.
The CBC as a national institution must be there for all Canadians and must continue to represent the views of all.
As for the clause itself, there has been no indication whatsoever that the concerns of the government and the bill are founded in fact. Specifically, there is no threat that the CBC will be an instrument of the state. The intention and the effect are for the CBC to be an instrument of the people, of society, of the Canadian nation, not-and I cannot stress this enough-the government or the state.
The government's reasoning is clearly suspect in this regard. One only has to read the remarks of the CBC's long-time president, Pierre Juneau, to realize there is no threat to the objectivity of the CBC or to any part of its continued effective broadcasting in this country. Monsieur Juneau has gone on record as saying that the national unity phrase had not caused any problems during his tenure at the CBC.
The CRTC has concurred with this position. The simple fact is that the clause in question has never precluded the effectiveness of the CBC in fulfilling its over-all mandate.
The CBC has historically been a unifying force in this country and should continue to be given this responsibility as a central aspect of its mandate. Removing this aspect from the CBC's purview would be a significant detriment to the corporation and the country. It amounts to the disembowelment of the CBC as a national institution.

Sixty years ago Prime Minister R. B. Bennett said that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as he helped to found it, would be an instrument of national consciousness and unity. He said that it was needed to bring the country together in those difficult times. He recognized that Canada's autonomy and independence hinged on the control of our communications system. Has really that much changed over the intervening years? I do not think so. The need is still as great as ever for a national institution to act as a unifying force.
I would argue that they are needed now more than ever before in our Canadian history. We need the CBC to act as a bulwark against the various decentralizing forces that bombard Canada from all its comers, from inside and outside this country, even from within this very House of Commons, from within this Parliament of Canada.
Canadians have diverse backgrounds and lives and so it is particularly important for federal institutions like the CBC to act as a unifying force, pulling Canadians together through the promotion of our common interests and perspectives.
National radio programs such as Momingside, As It Happens. Sunday Morning, Cross Country Check-Up-, as well as television shows like The National, The Journal, documentaries like Patrick Watson's The Struggle for Democracy, Ken Dryden's Home Game, and even Hockey Night in Canada provide a unifying influence on Canadians.
I am sure that this would continue at least in the short term without the national unity mandate specifically spelled out. But the focus might change. Over time the CBC could lose its effectiveness as a pro-Canadian force.
Some more cynical analysts have said that this bill in its present form could be the government's first step toward privatization of our beloved Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Any move in this direction would be tragic. The vast majority of Canadians believe that they have an incredible service at their disposal and would shun any move toward changing the 60-year mandate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
It is incumbent upon us here today to make a stand with these initial signs of erosion. The Mulroney govem-
Govemment Orders
ment has already cut the CBC's budget with abandon and disregard. We have seen this time and time again. We cannot also allow them to take away the fundamental mandate of the CBC through this flawed legislation.
It is clear that this bill must have changes made. The amendments we consider today, therefore, must be accepted in order to make broadcasting law in this country reflect the needs of this nation.
Broadcasting provides a unique opportunity to bind us together. It must not be ignored or tossed aside, especially at this time in the country's history when Canada is being pulled apart from many sides.
It is particularly ironic to me that the Prime Minister of Canada has named Keith Spicer to head a Citizens' forum intended to promote national unity, but he supports a broadcast bill that so fundamentally contradicts his expressed concern about national unify.
If the government is as eager to promote unity as it would like Canadians to believe, it can start by amending Bill C-40 and not so easily dispense with the essential mandate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
In conclusion, this act is so fundamentally flawed that it cannot, and must not, go through without amendment. As written, Bill C-40 precludes the CBC the opportunity to explore the vision of being an agency of national consciousness and of contributing the vital component, the national sounding board, for our common thoughts, interests and ideals.
This is a tragedy that must be corrected by those of us assembled here in this House of Commons. Therefore, I urge the government to support this critical amendment and to re-establish more substantial support for the CBC.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this very important debate. It is a debate, I feel, which proposes to alter the very foundation of the Canadian broadcasting system.
I am deeply concerned by most aspects of this destructive bill, but what disturbs me most is the clause which would remove from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the mandate to contribute to the development of national unity and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity.

November 29, 1990
Government Orders
The promotion of national unity has been a principle of the CBC since its foundation. If there ever was a time to eliminate this principle, this is the worst possible time.
Almost 60 years ago, Prime Minister R. B. Bennett said that the CBC would be an instrument of national consciousness and unity. I believe that the CBC has fulfilled that mandate and that to deny it the means and the will to continue doing so is a tragic mistake.
The CBC has acted as a unifying force throughout its existence. For many, if not all of us here today, the CBC and Radio-Canada played a major role in our lives as we grew up and continues to do so today. Before television and in many cases beyond, the radio was the best source of popular entertainment and information to be had by Canadians. There was an immediacy about radio, a sense of participation and presence that was lacking even in newspapers, and was highly valued.
Television is the dominant medium in the world today and the CBC has demonstrated its ability to stay at the forefront with innovative programming and bold initiatives such as the all news channel Newsworld. But while doing so, it has not neglected radio. Any fan of Morning-side, or As It Happens, or any number of other fine programs can attest to this.
CBC programming, both radio and television, serves to bring Canadians together, to teach us about each other. We are a small population scattered over a huge expanse of territory, and the challenge of communication is a major one. The CBC has played a vital role in ensuring that Canadians communicate with one another, that they feel connected to one another. This is especially true of Canadians living in the outlying and isolated areas of Canada. For them in particular the CBC is and always has been a strong and badly needed link to their fellow Canadians and to the world. For the bulk of the Canadian population densely clustered along the 49th parallel and the Great Lakes, the CBC serves to acquaint them with the other Canadian experience.
If not for the powerful voice of CBC many Canadians would be more familiar with the United States than they would be with their own country. To allow this to happen would be to weaken the bonds and the potential of this nation. To do what we can to familiarize Canadians with their own culture with their fellow citizens, is not to
promote "intolerable propaganda" as the Minister of Communications would have us believe, it is to provide Canadians with the opportunity to learn about each other, an opportunity they would not otherwise have.
The Prime Minister has stated that everything we have accomplished as a country can be traced back to our sense of national purpose, to our national unity. That is the very essence of the reason why national unity must remain a part of the CBC's mandate. It is not there to force the CBC and Radio-Canada to act as a propaganda machine for the state. If that were the result of the mandate surely this government, with its low standing in the polls, would want to keep it. It is not there to force the CBC to relay the news with a state or even a Canadian bias. Rather, the mandate to promote national unity is vital in an intangible way.
A sense of national purpose is badly lacking in Canada today and national unity seems very fragile. If the mandate to promote unity has been some kind of iron fist wielded by CBC, I have yet to see the results. That does not mean that eliminating the mandate is a trivial or meaningless action, one that should hardly cause a ripple. Indeed, we need that mandate more than ever. It can do no harm and it could be of great help. Canada is becoming more and more decentralized, economically, socially, culturally, linguistically, regionally, and even spiritually. We are pulling apart at the seams. The CBC has the potential to serve as a bulwark against these decentralizing forces but only if we allow it the means and the will to do so, and only if we have the willingness to listen and to learn.
A mandate to promote national unity: Those are not empty words but a statement of purpose and the articulation of a dream. We are a nation built on dreams. Many Canadians are descendants of those who came from across the sea seeking a better life.
The national railway which allowed westward expansion was bom in the imagination of a few men. For a nation such as this, a statement of purpose such as the promotion of national unity by CBC is not only necessary, it is natural.
We desperately need a sense of unity. We need a sense of national purpose. We need a sense that there is something worth fighting for. What kind of message does the elimination of the national unity mandate send to Canadians? It is a terribly negative message, and this is
November 29, 1990

the worst of all possible times for the federal government to be issuing negative messages.
Most of us in this House believe that Canada is worth fighting for, and I believe that most Canadians feel that way too. In the fight, we need a purpose. We need rallying cries. To gut our national broadcasting institution of its mandate to promote Canadians unity is to tell Canadians that the dream is dead.
In saying these things, I speak from the heart. There are other aspects of the government's proposal to eliminate the national unity mandate, and indeed aspects of the entire bill which disturb me in a more concrete way. I fear that there is an underlying message in Bill C-40, and that is the end of the CBC as a government funded institution.
Since 1984, this government has cut the CBC's parliamentary grants by over $240 million, including severe reductions to its high-tech equipment. The government does not seem dedicated or even interested in developing the CBC's great potential. That is what the government did to passenger rail in Canada. It killed it bit by bit.
I am afraid that is what is happening to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The presence of the federal government in rural Canada and in the regions is decreasing. Post offices are closing. Military bases have been scaled down or closed, such as CFB Summerside in my province of Prince Edward Island.
The government's obsession with the free market is causing it to sell off Crown corporations such as Air Canada and Petro-Canada. The government's presence in the areas of transportation and natural resources allowed Canadians some measure of control over the forces which affect their lives.
The same is true of communications. Given this track record, and given the contents and the tone of Bill C-40, I cannot help but suspect that the government intends to gradually abandon the CBC. Canadians in smaller and more remote population areas such as Prince Edward Island fear that their local stations, CBC Charlottetown, for example, will be among the first to go.
Rumours to that effect have been circulating for some time now, and with Bill C-40, they grow stronger. The people of Charlottetown and of P.E.I. for one would like
Government Orders
this government to promise that they will not lose their publicly funded CBC, which has served them well for so long.
To vote for the passage of Bill C-40 is to condone and to assist the government's plans for the CBC, none of which are good. If we have any remaining doubt about the government's attitude toward this most Canadian of institutions, we need only to think of its intention to eliminate the promotion of national unity from the CBC mandate. That says it all.
This aspect alone of Bill C-40 is a tacit admission by the federal government that it believes Canadian unity to be a dead dream. So far as it is concerned, the fabric of this country has been tom beyond repair.
Either that, or this government does not believe that Canada is in need of unifying symbols, statements or ideals. I strongly disagree with both of these. I believe that by sending such a negative message to Canadians, the federal government is abandoning its responsibility to do everything within its power to keep this country together and to make it strong.
"To contribute to the development of national unity and to provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity." Those words do not pose any threat to the freedom of the media. They have not had that effect in the past, and they will not have it in the future. What they have done is represent what we value most about the CBC, which is that it provides us with a mirror reflecting back both the good and the bad, allowing Canadians to continue to examine and re-evaluate ourselves and our nation, and to ponder what Canada is and what it can be.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to speak, however briefly, to Bill C-40, an Act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication. I am glad to see the Minister of Communications is here today to listen to the most fundamental aspect of this legislation which concerns Canada's national unity. I would like to start by congratulating the hon. member for Mount Royal on her excellent work on this bill and on what she did to clarify for Canadians the national unity aspect that

Government Orders
forms the nucleus of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's mandate in Canada.
Today, I will make my comments in French, and I do so for a very specific reason. Although my last name is LeBlanc, French is not my mother tongue, but I went to Quebec in the early 80s, when the national unity question was a subject of lively debate, especially in the province of Quebec. I was there as a student, to learn French, in an environment where this fundamental question that goes to the heart of our nation was very topical indeed.
I must say that my experience during those four years was a very valuable one, especially from a cultural point of view, because of the friendships I made and also because I was able to learn and understand a little more about the culture, values and principles of a society in this country that is very proud of what it has accomplished during the past three or four centuries, and which at that time was intent on discovering its identity.
I had an opportunity, since this was another critical period in our history, to see things from the perspective of a student at Laval University in Quebec City. I often watched CBC television to know what was going on across the country, and I saw that in Quebec as well, there was this yearning for an identity. Even out there, I realized there was, nevertheless, a national presence, a national government that recognized the aspirations of people in that part of Canada but at the same time did not intend to give way to these divided factions. It met them head-on and used the means at its disposal to tell Quebecers: Your future is in Canada.
This message has failed to come across since 1984. This government's statements and the messages and signals it sends are increasingly lacking in substance. One of the most discouraging indications of this lack of leadership, this failure to express our national identity, is the clauses we find in Bill C-40 before the House today. The purpose of the motion before the House today is to try and reverse this trend.
Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that if we believe in this country, we, as Canadians make an effort to reverse these trends and start speaking out to say that our country is Canada. We must defend our values and take pride in them.
If we start diluting the legislation that defines the mandate of our national broadcasting institution by saying that French and English are represented by two different communities or that national unity is no longer an important part of the mandate of our national television network, we are sending a message that the national government and our national institutions have lost the will and the courage to defend our country.
It is even more regrettable today, in 1990, when we look at other parts of the world and realize what we have here in Canada, compared with the situation in other countries around us.
Since I was elected, Mr. Speaker, I had a chance to visit Canada from coast to coast, not just Quebec and Western Canada but also the North. Every visit, every trip fills me with wonder at the splendour and riches of this country, and I ask myself what we can contribute to the world. We cannot help, however, if we are beset by internal divisions, if we are afraid to speak with a national voice and if we let ourselves be tom in so many directions. We cannot contribute effectively, for instance, toward resolving conflicts in the Middle East or help draft resolutions or rebuild a new world in the Soviet Union or elsewhere, as in the Third World, for instance.
I repeat, I am convinced that one area where Canada has a very important contribution to make is the environment. However, if we are distracted by internal divisions and are afraid to speak out, and if our government fails to give us any leadership in this field, we will be unable to make that contribution. The twenty-first century, which was to be Canada's century, will pass us by, and that would be regrettable for us here in Canada and even more so for people in other countries throughout the world.
These considerations go straight to the heart of the motions before the House today which are a particular concern of my colleague, who worked so hard to improve this bill in committee.
Mr. Speaker, one of our great Canadian philosophers was Marshall McLuhan, who had so much to say and contributed to our thinking about the media and communications in what he called the global village. McLuhan said: The medium is the message. He said the world had become a global village, mostly because of television. Television has caused the world to shrink and thus made it possible for us to express common values. However,
November 29, 1990

television can also be a source of division, separation and discord inside a country.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would like to say that Canada should stop acting like a young man who is perfectly healthy but all of a sudden decides to throw in the towel because life is no longer worthwhile and the challenges are too great. That is the general impression given by our national malaise. In fact, it is not a bad simile: this dynamic young man, who all of sudden feels that the challenges and opportunities of the future are just too much of a responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, they are not too much for us. What we need is time and a government that is prepared to pursue every avenue, to show leadership and to take a strong position in all areas, and that will start by improving the mandate we give our national telecommunications institution, which is why we are here today.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this subject on which I am very far from being a specialist, but I have become very concerned about it quite recently, partly from an experience I had last week, which I will mention.
The point of this amendment is that we should restore the principle that part of the CBC's mandate is to contribute to national unity as well a shared national consciousness or identity. It is very unfortunate that the government has undertaken to take out from the original mandate prior to the bill the duty to promote national unity.
If the objection is that it would be government propaganda, there are ways to deal with that so long as the duty is clearly defined because the government is only one of the governments in Canada. Unity does not mean uniformity, that everybody thinks the same, that everybody speaks the same language, that everybody wears the same clothes or supports the same hockey team. Unity means-especially in a country like Canada-unity of diverse groups that find how we can fit together and enrich each other. In other words, a very important part of a national broadcasting corporation should be to help the different regions and the different groups in Canada to know each other by letting them participate. That
Government Orders
should be part of the duty and it should be clearly stated under the obligation to promote national unity.
The reason I want to speak on this is that last weekend I happened to have two interesting but somewhat distressing conversations. One was with an old friend in rural Ontario. He is an anglo. Frankly, he is not very sympathetic with francophones in Ontario, or in Quebec, and he gave me some of his reasons why.
I was a little alarmed at the distance between him and me on that subject because I felt he did not know a great deal about what actually goes on in Quebec, about how the people live in Quebec in the most simple ordinary sense.
This person is a retired trade unionist from the factory in which I used to work where I was the secretary at one time and he the union president. He is a man of social responsibility. But what he does not know about the French people of Canada, especially in Quebec, limits his sympathy, and he is worried about national unity. He gets quite upset in saying that he would fight to stop anyone from splitting Canada in two. He means it. He does not intend to be hostile. He thinks that there are some hostile people over there. That was Saturday evening.
On Sunday evening I was speaking with another old friend in Montreal, again a manual worker and a person with a good deal of education and self-education. Unfortunately for me he is bilingual. He is francophone but fortunately much more bilingual than I. He was shocked at how little I know about what is going on recently in Quebec regarding certain briefs to the Belanger-Cam-peau Commission and so on.
We see each other several times a year. I live in Toronto and in Ottawa. My background is in Winnipeg and central Ontario, except for a very few years in Quebec. He feels that my understanding of him is very limited. He describes himself, and rightly so, as a federalist. He is aware of a separatist tide in Quebec, and he is very worried about it. He does not want our country split. He is distressed that I know so little, in his opinion, of the things in Quebec that matter to him.
Personally my situation is rather comical. I am in the middle between my anglophone friend in rural Ontario and my francophone friend in Montreal. I do not mean to blame any institution or any action, but the point is that we need the kind of institution that can explain the south to the north, the north to the south, Quebec to

I am very sorry that over the past five years the CBC's operating budget has been cut every year. In 1984-85 it was $943.3 million. Part of the programming that has been deleted because of those cuts is the regional programming, telling the north about the south, the south about the north, and the east about the west.
I am luckier than many Ontarians. I have been able to visit the maritimes sometimes and the west coast sometimes. For the most part, I do not know the maritimes. I have a son in Newfoundland, but I only see a little bit of Newfoundland when I visit there.
The programs on the CBC are very valuable. It is unfortunate that many of those very Canadian programs-and by that I do not mean uniformly Canadian; I mean Newfoundland, Vancouver, Yukon, northern Ontario, the Eastern Townships of Quebec, or many other groups-have been cut back. It is very unfortunate that CBC has been, by the budget cuts, pressured to abandon its goal of 95 per cent Canadian content in prime time.
Prime time is pretty important, especially for our children as they are growing up; in my case our grandchildren. They have to have the chance to watch these Canadian content programs when they should not be in bed or at school.
There is nothing we can do today, in this bill, about the budget cuts, but we can at least, if the government will see the point, restore the principle that the CBC has a duty to promote national unity. We have heard a great
deal during the past year or two about the need for national unity.
It is very unfortunate and strange, and for some people it is very offensive, that at the time the Prime Minister speaks about national unity his government is demolishing, piece by piece, slice by slice, budget cut by budget cut, and now with legislative changes, one of the main instruments of national unity created by the Canadian people.
Whether the government is planning to sell off the CBC in whole or in part, I do not know of course. It has done that with many other groups created by the Canadian taxpayers and labour, often sold at a ridiculously small price. What its plans are for the CBC, it has not told us yet. It should not take out of the law this duty to promote national unity, or else the Prime Minister will have to be seen by Canadian people as not meaning what he says when he talks about national unity.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to rise in the House today to address Bill C-40 respecting broadcasting and amendments to certain acts.
I would like to direct my comments to the whole issue of national unity. I come from an area that represents a mosaic of Canadians. First Canadians are in the majority in the area that I represent, and basically these people have their own languages and their own cultures. This a reflection of Canada and what Canada is all about.
Bill C-40 drops the CBC's 1968 mandated role to contribute to the development of national unity and to provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity. My feeling is that the removal of the national unity reference was recommended by both the Caplan-Sauva-geau report in 1986 and the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture in 1987.
The standing committee had been concerned that this clause might interfere with CBC's ability to ensure that its programming reflect and interpret as fully, as fairly and as accurately as possible Canada's cultural, social, political, economic, linguistic and regional reality and diversity.
Former CBC President Pierre Juneau told the standing committee that the phrase national unity had not

caused any problems during his years at the CBC. The CRTC noted that its interpretation of the term never precluded a free political discussion from all points of view.
Coming from the Northwest Territories and from an area that is highly represented by a multiplicity of factors which lead to a very diverse population of languages and cultures, my feeling is that the systematic dismantling of the CBC will have serious effects on the quality of our lives as Canadians.
Local news broadcasts may have to be cancelled. Some regional radio stations will have to close. Commercials will have to be reintroduced on CBC radio. The current level of regional programming cannot be maintained. This is particularly serious in the north because we depend on information which is critical to our safety, such as on the weather and flying conditions.
Liberal members of Parliament believe that because our country is so vast we need a sufficiently funded CBC in order for the whole country to have access to this service.
The CBC unites our country. It is precisely because the CBC is a public network that it can offer wholly Canadian programming. By destroying the CBC, the government is destroying an important part of Canadian culture. Canadians have moulded the CBC over the past 50 years into the quality Canadian programming of today. What justification does the government have for reversing all this in one fall swoop?
If we are to preserve our identity as a nation, we need to invest in our cultural institutions. I believe the government, by cutting funding to the CBC, is ensuring that our children will grow up with less than a true sense of what it is to be Canadian and what Canada is all about.
We know that many Canadians share our concern about the impacts the cuts will have on the CBC and on Canadians. It is essential that we tell the government loudly and clearly that it is not acceptable to destroy and erode the public broadcasting program of Canada.
I feel so strongly about the CBC and the role it plays in educating Canadians about Canadians that I wrote to Patrick Watson and Gerard Veilleux in February to ask why they do not provide the Newsworld service and if

they would provide the news world service to the Northwest Territories.
We were hosting a major leadership forum which focused on national issues, issues of national importance and ones which particularly referred to issues of aboriginal populations across Canada. There was much reference to Arctic sovereignty. There was reference to the whole issue of self-government.
These are things that Canadians want to know about. It would be important for the whole nation to have seen this, and this is what I wrote to Mr. Watson and Mr. Veilleux. In part I wrote:
Sovereignty is important to all Canadians but it is the residents of the Arctic who have maintained the north's sovereignty through traditional use and occupancy of the land and water. What political development means with or without the Meech Lake Accord is unique to the two territories. Environment issues in the Arctic are different than those in other areas. Energy is equally important. The north has the resources to make Canada energy self-sufficient. I could go on but my point is that the forum this weekend will be dealing with many profound problems that would be extremely educational and interesting for all Canadians.
I want to provide this House with at least part of the response I received from these two very honourable gentlemen, because it indicates the belief of CBC management with respect to the role that CBC plays in national unity. It is important for me to share this with the House. Mr. Veilleux wrote: "The CBC fully recognizes the importance of bringing concerns of northern Canadians to the attention of the whole country. Indeed, with respect to Newsworld in particular, every weekend we broadcast Focus North from Yellowknife and Mayda from Whitehorse. Regularly throughout the week we have inserts from Yellowtaiife into our prime time Calgary program This Country".
He continued: "In closing, I wish to stress that the advent of Newsworld has heralded a dramatic increase in the coverage of the political agenda of Canada. It has also brought an unprecedented level of regional coverage to all parts of the country. What is more, the region that has benefited most from our formats and our editorial imperative to show Canadians other parts of Canada is the north. Never before have northern concerns been so presented so frequently and so directly, and without being filtered through a central and southern Canadian perspective".

Page 6 of the bill indicates that programming which reflects aboriginal cultures of Canada should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system as resources become available for the purpose. This is the statement of commitment within the body of this bill. I have here a couple of press releases from the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation. In one of these press releases, a lady by the name of Blandina Makik, Executive Producer of Children's Programming in Iqaluit, in the Northwest Territories, calls the $600,000 cut to the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation spiritual genocide. She states that the cuts are expected to be felt in cultural, educational, news and current affairs programs, broadcast in Inuktitut to homes where many of the older Inuit do not speak English. Essentially, the reference is to a unilingual group.
The other thing which is quite devastating for this particular area is that in the $600,000 cut was included a very, very important program called The Super Shmoo series, which had a funding of $215,000. The native communications programs were cut back and this does not do anything for national unity. It does not give the complete expression of language and culture of all regions of Canada.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that Canada is a cultural mosaic, and we are more influenced than any other nation by our vast geography and vast wilderness and by our environment. Part of what has helped to build our country, from east to west and to the north is our infrastructure, such as the public broadcasting system. We have enforced a sense of Canadianism in ourselves through the CBC, which helps define a sense of our own
identity as a nation. So now, more at this time in history than any other time, we need this institution of national unity to speak to one another.

Mr. Speaker, I am extremely pleased to be able to speak to this legislation today. Frankly, if we want to be serious about national unity, and I believe that every single Canadian in his or her own way wants to be, we have to think very seriously about our national institutions. One of these is communications, and certainly we have to think equally seriously about the importance of restoring the national unity clause.
Many of us are particularly preoccupied with what is happening in the country today. We recognize the great conflicts and the great pressures in the country. When we think about national unity, surely we need to acknowledge that every single man and woman needs to feel as if they can get what is their fair share from this country. Canadians, whether of aboriginal ancestry, French, English, or other ancestry, needs to feel as if they belong and they count. The five to seven million functionally illiterate Canadians need to believe that they can improve their lot and participate more fully in Canadian society. Every poor Canadian of the more than five million poor in this country needs to believe as well that he or she will break out of this vicious circle of poverty.
Until all of our regions, whether in the great north or in the western provinces, Ontario, Quebec or the Atlantic provinces feels that it will be treated fairly, that there are mechanisms in place that will help it to communicate, help it to work out its differences, we will not have the kind of strong united country that we want.



I would like to ask the government to stop dismantling what we have built, what unites us, to stop destroying the institutions that give us a chance to talk and get to know one another.

Let us look at some of the decisions that have been taken.

I believe that some of the decisions that have been made did not contribute anything at all to make Canada a strong and united country. Consider for instance the cut-backs at VIA Rail where more than 2,700 employees have been laid off, or the Air Canada privatization deal not long after that which was the end of the line for over 2,900 men and women. I am sure you remember the sale of Route Canada by the CN and that you are aware of the fact that nearly 2,000 men and women have been are still suffering because the government does not seem to be able to do anything to help them.
With respect to the privatization of Petro-Canada, we can see now that we had just the right organization which, had the government been willing to act, could have met the energy needs of all Canadians. Why did the government fail to come up with a policy. After all, we have had six years to achieve energy self-sufficiency.
Just looking at the number of bankruptcies, which are now at an all-time high, is enough to realize that the country is being tom apart and falling down. The government-created recession, a fact admitted by the ministers involved, is certainly not going to help strengthen national unity. Some of the CBC cut-backs- my colleague has just referred to them-have been driving Canadians even further apart, and this is true from one end of the country to the other.

What we really need to do is start listening to the people again. If we were to ask Canadians whether or not they want this government and this Parliament to make a sincere and profound commitment to national unity, we would get an unequivocal yes. People would be telling us to do everything in our power to make sure that the country is able to bounce back, that it is able to

become much more united and much stronger than it has ever been.
We need to start listening to Canadians, to its five million poor, most of whom are women, many of whom are seniors, about one million of whom are children. We need to start talking to and listening to the functionally illiterate Canadians, who number between five million and seven million, and who feel sometimes as if they will never be able to break out of this difficulty that they are experiencing. Disabled Canadians often feel marginalized. We are talking about 3.3 million Canadians. We have to start listening to all of them in all regions of Canada from each and every single province and each of our two territories.
The removal of this particular clause is another blow, another kick, another shot, if you like, at Canada. It will damage the concept of national unity, which is so precious and so essential to a nation such as ours, particularly one as large and complex and so vast that many, many Canadians do not understand it nearly as well as they should or could.
I ask the government to consider the restoration of the national unity clause. We need to admit that we need information about ourselves. We know too little about each other, and because we know so little, we often misunderstand each other.
Let me complete my address by simply using an analogy. If a family is going to be strong and united, it needs good information within that family. We need open communications. We need to know each other so that we can reach out to each other.

The members of a strong and united family talk to each other. We need to have open and honest exchanges that will make it easier to understand one another, to work and play together and contribute to our unity. I believe the same is true of a country like ours. Without sound information about other Canadians from the various regions and without open communication lines we will not go very far.

With those particular comments, I will ask the government to ensure that it looks at this particular clause, that it makes sure that the tools that we, as Canadians, need to build a stronger more united country are, in fact, given to us. I believe most of us would agree that until every single man, woman and child in this great nation,
