Mr. Speaker, broadcasting, whether it is television or radio, brings Canada and the world into our living rooms. It brings in a world of news, sports, entertainment and public affairs. Broadcasting is a key medium which unites us by reflecting Canada to our fellow Canadians at a time when unifying the country is more critical than ever before, given the deep divisions and racial intolerance that are dividing so many communities.
Given these realities, Liberals believe that Bill C-40 moves away from the strong national broadcasting system that Canada has always held as part of this elusive Canadian identity, letting us share a common purpose. For this reason, we believe the government is wrong to weaken the CBC in its proposed broadcasting legislation.
With the passage of Bill C-40, the CBC will no longer be required to contribute to the development of national unity. It will be dropped from its mandate, just when the government should be doing everything in its power to give each and every Canadian a true sense of belonging and participation. For us on this side of the House, our goal for Canada is developing a national personality, building a sense of national unity and a national consciousness. We believe we need a strong national institution like the CBC to weave all of the regions and all of the diverse participants of Canada into a united nation that is working in the interests of all Canadians.
Just last spring we in the rural communities across this countiy lost a valuable resource in the agricultural community. We lost George Price, one of CBC radio's last farm reporters. His position had been cut. I strongly
disagree with this decision. We already miss George Price.
He has been an excellent agri-food industry reporter. However, even though George Price is no longer with us, what is more important is the CBC has eliminated his position. The farmers of Canada who have relied on this information service for input on agricultural issues will have a grave loss. Farmers do not have the time to catch regularly scheduled newscasts but they always listened to George Price and his program while driving their tractors or their combines in the fields.
Yet, in the response from the CBC when I wrote about this they pointed out that farmers get up-to-the-minute information from computers, fax machines, wire services, all news television and a variety of other sources, as well as CBC radio. The did not see CBC radio as a loss.
I have to point out that I am not only a member of this House, but I am also a farmer. Certainly we have some of the services I have just listed in our homes, but we do not have them on our tractors and our combines, other than the radio. George Price's program was something we never missed, whether we were on the tractor, the combine or in our homes. He was one of the few reporters who was factual, he was on the job and he kept the other elements of the news media honest. George Price was a very conscientious person who always gave an unbiased account of what was happening.
I have to compare this with some of the headlines over the last few weeks. Some of that was instituted in the House of Commons, when the minister of trade chastised the Minister of Agriculture for giving the farmers $8.8 billion in subsidies, which was a concocted figure. We had a headline saying, "Lavish farm subsidies milking consumers", and of course the poor reporter did not know if that was a factual figure.
George Price would never have let them get away with that.
Another one from the Montreal Gazette: "Farmers being dragged kicking and screaming into the 1990s." This is an account of a report put together by the Canadian Consumers' Association. They say that Canadians paid double the average world price for milk

because of restrictions that protect the domestic dairy industry from cheaper imports.
That reporter, and obviously the newspaper, did not realize that input costs are higher here in Canada. They seem to think the farmers are getting the extra indirect subsidies.
Even The Globe and Mail, November 19: "The policy panel" by a former Deputy Minister of Finance of this government and also a former president of a bank, compared the $2.7 billion subsidies to marketing boards as an indirect subsidy from the consumers to the producer.
He did not stop to realize that input costs here in Canada are 25 to 30 per cent higher than they are in the United States. I countered to him that perhaps we could look at the interest rates. This is a former bank president. Interest rates are higher in Canada than in the United States.
I have to ask you, Mr. Speaker, if it necessarily follows that Canadian milk prices are higher than they are in the United States and so are Canadian interest rates, are the banks not being subsidized by the consumers and small businesses and big business.
Let's follow that theory through and be fair and honest. If George Price was there again, they would never have gotten away with it.
To top it all, here we have some massive cuts in CBC's budget. Yet, this government funded the Canadian Consumers' Association with $790,000 to come out with a report as inaccurate as this, obviously displaying a double standard.
Other businesses in society must have a profit to survive. Agriculture is no different. If it does not have that profit, then the whole industry is going down the tubes. I can never remember a time, even back into the 1930s when I first remember going to town with my dad for supplies, when things were as tough as they are out there at the present time, and this government is completely insensitive.
Mr. Speaker, I have to tell you that this country is going to hold this government accountable not only for the cuts it made to the CBC but for what is going to happen five years down the road. We know what is happening in Russia at the present time. There are food shortages there.

Their system of corporate farming did not survive, and it is not going to survive here in Canada. If George Price was still in the CBC, he would be reminding the government and the people of Canada that the farmers, too, deserve an income that is commensurate with the rest of that of society or they are not going to survive.
When I look at what has been happening here with this government, it does not really seem to care about any of our national institutions. It simply wants to promote the world trade at the cost of those institutions in Canada that served us well over the years. It has ignored the reasons behind the need for the Canadian Wheat Board when it was brought in by a Conservative government back in the 1930s.
It has ignored why the Canadian Dairy Commission was brought into being. It has ignored the reasons why the Egg Marketing Agency, the Broiler Marketing Agency and the Titrkey Marketing Agency were brought into being. It forgot the chicken and egg wars. It forgot the other things that happened in history that brought about the creation of these institutions.
Institutions were always accurately reported by George Price, not like the garbage that we have been hearing in last six weeks from the concerted media attack on these institutions that have served this country so well. I have to wonder who is orchestrating these attacks, because the Minister of Agriculture has been very quiet on the whole issue.
As a matter of fact, in a meeting last week in Winnipeg, one of the senior officials of Canada Agriculture in charge of policy stated that perhaps the consumers should be setting the price of milk. What is going to happen if they are going to insist on setting the price of milk? Will they set the price or our input costs too? Are they going to set the price of what you have to purchase as a consumer?
I think not. I want an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture as to why he is letting one of his officials state these types of policies that are surely going to establish a double standard. Or, is he going to move to the corporate farms? I think this House deserves an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture and from that official.
This Conservative government since 1984 has cut CBC's parliamentary grants by over $240 million, which includes severe reductions to our high-tech equipment. Certainly, the CBC should be made a vehicle for promoting Canadian unity, more so than the other institutions that we have in society. It must remain that

I want to reiterate that such a drastic cut to the position such as George Price held is not acceptable to this side of the House. I urge strongly to have that taken into consideration and have it reinstated as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the record shows that I follow several speakers from this side of the House who have expressed profound concern for the future of the Canadian broadcasting system.
Let the record also show that the Conservatives, on the other side of the House, have not taken part in this debate. That includes the hon. Minister of Communications who sits at his desk and refuses to come to the defense of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I say shame on the Minister of Communications. I say shame on the whole lot of you.
We are here today involved in what I would describe as a very strange debate. It is strange because it deals with a clause in Bill C-40, this broadcast bill, that will take away the national unity mandate from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It seems that only in Canada can we have this kind of occurrence. We have a cherished and treasured public broadcasting system which has done a tremendous job for more than half a century. It has been as important to this country as the railway that was built from coast to coast well over a century ago.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has played an absolutely crucial and indispensable role in the development of Canada. It was a noble idea from the beginning and it is still a noble idea. A public broadcast corporation like the CBC reflects the country and ties us together. After all, this is a huge sparsely-populated country. The CBC reflects Canada. It tells us about our woes, our dreams, our controversies and our hurts. The CBC reflects most everything that is Canada.
We now come to this clause in Bill C-40. If it goes through-and Tories are pretty good at ramming things through-it will remove the national unity mandate from the CBC, as if it were some kind of disease. The argument that this government has put forward with respect to taking away the national unity mandate is that it is concerned about turning the corporation into some kind of propaganda machine. It would not want to have
the CBC behaving as if it were some kind of a propaganda outlet.
I worked at the CBC for 18 years. I think that I know something about the corporation. I can assure you that if you leave the national unity mandate with the CBC, it is not going to be in any way in the future a propaganda machine.
Let us get an understanding of the CBC because I think this is where the Tories go wrong. They do not understand the function of the CBC. They do not understand the kind of work the CBC does. The CBC is much more than just a news disseminating agency. If the CBC was just gathering, writing, editing and delivering the news, perhaps I could question the national unity mandate because reporters are an independent-minded people, they really do not care about politics. They are concerned about delivering the news, good or bad.
The CBC is so much more than that. It is a national broadcasting institution that ties the entire country together and reflects the Canadian story. That takes resources. It is an enormous job and I think it is the responsibility of the government to say to the corporation that part of its job is national unity, not by twisting the news or concocting some kind of silly political story, but by doing the job. It takes a lot of resources and an enormous amount of commitment to carry out the national unity task. That is why the government should be standing behind the CBC and telling the CBC that it is a force for national unity.
Let me use an analogy, Mr. Speaker. If we did not have a CBC television or radio outlet in the province of Manitoba, could one not make the argument that that is not good for national unity? I would suggest to you that if the national public broadcast system ignored one of the provinces, I do not think it would be very good for national unity. I think it would be right and proper for the government to tell the CBC that it wants an outlet in the province of Manitoba for it to do the job that the CBC is charged to do.
When it comes to the matter of national unity, if the CBC is charged with that mandate it can then turn to the government to say that it needs resources to do its job. It might mean more news editors, producers, and directors in the province of British Columbia. It might even mean needing more entertainment programs. Whatever it is, it

is all part and parcel of this job in the name of national unity.
Let us forget about the nonsense of propaganda. We are not talking about propaganda, we are talking about the corporation doing its job. When the CBC does a good job, be it news, entertainment, current affairs, Hymn Sing, it is all under the aegis of doing it for Canada, and therefore doing it for national unity.
By taking the national unity mandate away from the CBC, it sends a very bad signal. It sends a signal to certain people in the country who would like to Balka-nize, break up and separate the country into two countries. I do not think that is the responsibility of parliamentarians and certainly is not the responsibility of the federal government charged with operating a healthy CBC.
Mr. Speaker, how much time do I have left?

Perhaps I should not be very surprised by this proposal on the part of the government because this Conservative government does not have faith in public institutions anyway. Ironically, if the CBC were privately owned I would not be surprised if it had a mandate with respect to national unity, and we would not have this clause at all.
We would not have this clause in the bill because then the Tbries on that side of the House would say: "Ah well, they know what they are doing. If they need a national unity clause, so be it". But they do not have any faith in this public broadcast system. It is a dam, dam shame. It is a terrible shame.
Let me just finish by saying this: The Conservatives and this government like to spread the rumour that Canadians have lost faith in their institutions, and that includes the CBC. Not true. There was a recent survey in western Canada which shows once and for all that Canadians do have great faith in their institutions. It is just this government that spreads a lot of bad news which is not factual.

Mr. Speaker, I could have listened for days to my hon. colleague on his speech about the CBC. He is a distinguished broadcaster who certainly knows not just a lot about broadcasting, but about national unity.
I have the great occasion recently on a trip to western Canada to sit with him many afternoons, along with some distinguished western Canadians, to discuss issues such as national unity. It truly is too bad that we did not have unanimous consent of the House so that the House could benefit from his wisdom and experience.
I want to get right to the meat of the matter in dealing with the motion that is before us in Bill C-40, the broadcasting act. I grew up way down east. Anybody who listens to me in the House knows that I am veiy proud of where I come from. I am proud that I am a Canadian from Atlantic Canada. But when I was growing up there was a saying that my father used to quote often. It was: "If it ain't broke, don't fix it".
I have looked at the amendments being proposed here in Bill C-40. I cannot believe that a minister of the Crown and a government that claims to govern for all of Canada-not for just a part of it-would have the gall to remove a clause from a Crown corporation like CBC, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-Radio-Canada, which is a piece of national infrastructure. It is a piece of Canadiana.
Sure, there are a lot of things that should be improved in the broadcast bill. We have heard much debate on it. We probably will hear more before the day is over. But for the minister to propose to take out what I consider to be motherhood just blows me over. The minister indicated that he wants to take out the clause, and I will read it:

development of national unity and provide for continuing expression
of Canadian identity".

The minister found that so objectionable that he had to put a clause in the bill to remove it. He was quoted by the Toronto Globe and Mail on September 12, 1990, as saying that he found that 22-year old national unity mandate as intolerable interference because the CBC was maintaining this political valve artificially.
I think that is a bunch of hogwash. We are in a situation in this country because of the activity of this government since 1984, when it assumed power and told the Canadian public that it was fit to govern, that it would create great economic prosperity and wealth across this country, but most of all, that it could keep this country together.
Since 1984 we have seen this government on the front benches opposite not only wreak economic devastation from coast to coast to coast in this country, but to dismantle the-the minister is over there and I would hope that he would listen. He is a member of this government, as is the Minister of Communications.
What this government has done has systematically dismantled the national infrastructure of this country. Every instrument of national unity has been subject to attack, a battering, assault and battery by this government.
I cannot believe the Minister of Communications can sit there and read through his press clippings. No wonder he cannot look most of us in the face. I do not know what he thinks the mandate of the CBC should be. Should the mandate of the CBC be just a commercial endeavour? Should the mandate of the CBC be just to report the news as it is seen in Montreal and in Toronto? Well, I am a Canadian and I happen to come from the east coast of this country and I believe in this country.
That's their problem.
The Minister of Transport says that is my problem.
That's their problem.

If it is anybody's problem, it is your problem because you guys do not like what you hear most days from this side of the House because you cannot stand to hear the truth the way it is spoken on this side of the House.
Hear, hear.

I want to get into this thing about the national unity clause. I do not know if the minister really has a firm commitment to national unity in this country. He has under his ministry responsibility for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
He is from the province of Quebec, a province that currently is expressing some great reservations about the merit of staying in this country. It has established a commission of the provincial government to look at options as to whether or not they should stay in this country.
We hear all kinds of talk from the official opposition in Quebec City about sovereignty, or sovereignty association, and one of the main implements and instruments of national unity as mandated by statute is the CBC to promote Canadian unity. At this time in our history when the country is just about to fly apart, the Minister of Communications comes forward and is absolutely determined to remove the mandate of the CBC, one of the few remaining pieces of national infrastructure, threads of national unity. He wants to strip the mandate to promote Canada and understanding between Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I started off by saying that when I grew up my father told me that if it ain't broke, don't fix it. So I cannot quite get it through my head why this minister, when he is coming in with this bill which tampers with a whole lot of things with the Broadcast Act, felt so determined that he had to remove the mandate for national unity. I have read a lot of his statements and statements from people in the broadcast industry.
More important, I have listened to Canadians. I have listened to Canadians in the west, in Ontario, in Quebec, and in Atlantic Canada. Canadians are starting to wonder if this government really wants this country to stay together. Canadians are starting to wonder if ministers like the Minister of Communications really believes that this country is worth saving, really believes that this country can survive, or if what they are doing is trying to adjust the statutes of this country to a reality that they see, a reality of a country that is no longer together. Maybe it is a reality of a country unfortunately split along linguistic lines or geographic lines, but probably linguistic.
November 29, 1990

Government Orders
I am going to stay here to hear the minister, would like to hear a rousing defence of national unity, a strong federalist speech from this minister, dealing with communications and the role of the CBC and cultural institutions that come under his mandate, and promoting and preserving national unity in this country.
As well I hope everybody who is watching television stays tuned to the debate. I would like to know if this minister has given up on the concept of a strong federal country called Canada or if he has already thrown in the towel and is simply trying to adjust the current legislation on the federal books to reflect his view that there is more than one Canada, that there are two Canadas here.
The motion that has been put forward is one that everybody in this House should support. There comes a time when partisanship in this House has to give way to national good. In this particular case the amendment put forward reinstates into the Broadcasting Act that it be imperative that the CBC promote national unity. That is something that each and every individual in this House, male and female, east, west, central Canadian, French or English, should see as imperative these days when our country is being faced with such tugs and strains to the fabric of unity. I would hope that the ministers would review the program of systematic destruction of the fabric of national unity in this country and see that what this minister has proposed in Bill C-40, particularly this motion which we are debating now, is not only regressive but it is destructive, and see the danger that this particular clause causes and talk to the minister, before he gets up, and tell the minister that we need a speech of unity from him. What we do not need from this minister is more gobbledegook and-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret the hon. member's time has expired.

I cannot see why you would be so surprised, Mr. Speaker, because this is after all a debate that concerns all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to rise on this debate and, in particular, speak to the issue about which I think every Canadian should be thinking around this time of the year, Christmastime.
We are probably at a very critical time in the history of our country and we need leadership on a national level to help keep this country together. I happen to believe that as Canadians and, in particular, as parliamentarians too little is being said in this national Canadian Parliament about the values that we share together. One of those values is the capacity to communicate in our two official languages and the capacity to communicate by the instrument that links this country from coast to coast.
One of the reasons that I fear for the future of this country is because Canadians spend too little time communicating and speaking together. How many French Canadians know the names of Barbara Frum and Peter Mansbridge? How many English Canadians know the names of Denise Bombardier and Simon Durivage? If we are going to keep this country together, it is clear that we need instruments like the CBC to promote national unity. Marcel Masse, is that such a dirty word, to promote national unity?
I ask that because the minister has not had the courage to speak in the House to this issue, nor has his Prime Minister. At a time when the very future of this country is at stake, surely we can expect leadership on the national level to address these questions.
Quebecers have a right to ask themselves the question: is there anybody in this country who cares about whether they belong to Canada or not? That is the question that is being asked right now in the Belanger-Campeau commission. Whatever the outcome of that commission, they are examining their future in a serious, constructive, and complete way. I am sorry to say that the same cannot be said of our Prime Minister and the pathetic effort called the Spicer commission with commissioners working possibly two days a month, maybe two days a week, commissioners who do not have a mandate, and posts that are being left empty, a Prime Minister who is not even prepared to speak publicly to the Belanger-Campeau commission about the future that Quebec might still have within a country called Canada.

Government Orders

And the Minister of Communications stands there, looking unconcerned. That does not concern him that he is depriving us of one of the instruments of Canadian unity. If he wants to do away with Canada, he should say so. If we still want Canada after Meech, Mr. Speaker, we must be able to communicate with one another and, at least, instruments such as the CBC will ensure we can do jsut that. I am not referring to Clyde Wells's language, which I suggest is not so much a form of communicaton as a form of excommunication. I prefer to have language-

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point to the role of national unity that can be played by instruments like the CBC and Radio-Canada. I am not suggesting that there be journalistic gerrymandering. I worked as a journalist and heaven forbid that the government should tell journalists how to write. When Le Point and the CBC, in the weeks leading up to the Meech debate, developed a joint program where they explored the lives and reactions of Canadians, the very different views of the process leading up to the constitutional reform known as Meech Lake, it was clear that programs of that nature finally gave Canadians a chance to see how the other half felt.
How many English Canadians really understand why Quebec feels rejected, why Quebec is prepared, and possibly in the very near future, to give up on the country of Canada? We do not understand it, because even in our pan-Canadian news network called Newsworld we cannot hear the news in French. We can get the nightly news from Japan, but we do not have a French Canadian network through the Newsworld channel in the way that we should have.

One third of all Canadians are denied the right to listen to news in their own language. That is absolutely ridiculous, Mr. Speaker. During the Liberal leadership race, the leaders debate, in Montreal, had to be translated back into English to be broadcasted in the province of Quebec. You call that national broadcasting? That is ridiculous! Instead of using this bill to strenghten our means of communications, the minister is using it to deprive us of one of the last instruments at our disposal
to precisely touch the hearts of the Canadian people and more particularly in these times that of the people of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, it is not only the issue of the Canadian unity clause, but also the fact that the minister is not prepared to protect Radio Canada International, nor to specifically mention the parliamentary channel.

It is not only the issue related to the national unity objectives of the CBC, but also the fact that the Minister of Communications is not prepared to outline in law a mandate for the parliamentary channel. Surely, if there is one way that we are going to keep this country talking together, it is by virtue of channels like this parliamentary channel that permits Canadians from coast to coast to hear the laws of the land in both official languages.
Not only is the Minister of Communications giving up on Canadian unity, throwing in the towel on the capacity of Radio-Canada to act as an instrument of national unity, but he is further cutting back on Canada's view internationally by refusing to reinforce the role of Radio Canada International.
We know that there are cuts and that the other shoe is about to drop. We will see fewer and fewer Canadian messages being sent out to the world. Neither is he prepared to protect the parliamentary channel. Northern Services also was a portion of the CBC that should be protected by legislation, and he is unprepared to act.
If there is one thing that we are going to be able to do, it is going to be by communicating through the mass media. I hate to say it but Marshall McLuhan was right: the medium is the message. The medium that is the message of a very power nature today is the medium of television. It is clear that both radio and television in the CBC have a very important role to play in educating and teaching Canadians about one another.

And the role the CBC plays, Mr. Speaker, as a link between the people in Western Canada and in Eastern Canada, is a capital one that should be mentionned in the bill. I do not understand why the minister refuses to answer. Maybe he is too busy with his own cable tax which will cost millions of dollars to the people of Quebec, whose language he did not protect. He did not protect the French language when he imposed the same base tax rate to the people who never watch English
November 29, 1990

television. The minister, who talks so much of protection, missed the point in his own bill.

I am pleading with the minister to reconsider his position, to re-assert the capacity of the CBC to act as an instrument of national unity, and to make sure that the mandate of the CBC includes the notion of embracing not only our two cultural and linguistic groups that founded this country but also the one-third of Canadians who claim neither English nor French as their mother tongue. That must continue to be the respected and deserved mandate of the CBC.
I hope that, if he wants to have a say about the future of Canada, the minister is at least prepared to safeguard our means of communicating with one another in both official languages.

Mr. Speaker, it is not that I do not enjoy hearing the hon. member for Hamilton East, but our time this afternoon is running very short and I want to have an opportunity to speak to Bill C-40 and the amendment before us today put forward by the hon. member for Mount Royal concerning reinstating the mandate of CBC to have a national unity role. In fact, Motion No. 17 indicates that the CBC should contribute to national unity, shared national consciousness, and identity.
The fact that we are debating this issue in this year, 1990, is really remarkable. It is simply unbelievable that any government, especially this government, would be bringing forward this Bill C-40 which would take away the responsibility of the CBC to play a national unity role.
In my opinion the CBC has a unique position in this country. We have the ability of CBC radio and television,
Government Orders
but especially radio, to nip into every community right across this country, whether it is the outports of Newfoundland or the forestry communities of British Columbia or on the prairies or in Ontario or whatever. CBC radio has a special role and ability, whether it is This Country in the Mornings or the Gzowski Show, whether it is Cross Country Check-Up on Sunday afternoon, whether it is the As It Happens program at 6.30 in the evening, or a number of newscasts. There is practically no other instrument that knits this country together the way that CBC radio and CBC television do.
To take away this mandate of national unity from the CBC is really remarkable at a time when we have separatists sitting in the House of Commons, after going through the Meech Lake fiasco and after seeing a government that carries with it something like 14 per cent or 15 per cent support in the national public opinion polls.
It is incredible, when we have the Belanger-Campeau Commission looking at what role Quebec will play in the future of Canada, when similar commissions are being set up by other provinces and now that the Prime Minister has established the Citizens' Forum on the Future of Canada, that this government would be removing national unity as one of the mandates of the CBC. This is unbelievable. I would certainly hope that the Minister of Communications would agree. Regardless of what his previous thoughts were about Canada or even what they are now, surely the Prime Minister should put his foot down.
I was appalled and surprised today, when the former Conservative member from Nova Scotia put a question to the Prime Minister on whether he or the senior minister in his cabinet responsible for federal-provincial relations was going to make a presentation before the Belanger-Campeau Commission, that the Prime Minister looked dumbfounded. When a commission in Quebec is looking at the role of Quebec in the future of this country, surely the Prime Minister should go before that commission and put before it the federalist national view of this government with regard to unity, to a federal role for the Government of Canada, and to a national unity scheme to ensure that Quebec plays a vital role and that we are a united country.

November 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
I could not believe that he had no response. He fobbed it off by saying that there was a member from the caucus on the commission. It simply makes one wonder where this government really stands when it comes to national unity. I hope that the members of the Tory caucus will vote with their heads, their minds, their conscience, and their heart for Canada.
Surely this country and what it has done for each and every one of us is far more important than the Tory Party, the Liberal Party, the NDP, or any other party in this country. I would hope that the Tory members would vote with their conscience and with their hearts for Canada when this resolution comes before them sometime next week.
I want to speak as well about the unique role that I see for the CBC in this country, not only in national unity but in informing us of what is going on. Not very often do I have the opportunity to listen to programs like This Country in the Morning, but sometimes in the summertime and at times when the House is not sitting I do. It seems to me that it gives us a unique capsule of the problems of various parts of the country, what the people are thinking, and what the issues are. Private radio and television cannot do that. It is not something that can be done easily, but CBC radio has a unique capacity.
People who are posted abroad in Latin America, or I suppose in the Persian Gulf, and certainly our Armed Forces in Lahr and Baden-Baden in Germany tell me that being able to receive CBC Radio Canada International keeps them in touch with a feeling for not only their section of the country they come from but for the entire country.
I believe that CBC radio has a very special mandate to bind the country together in that way, to keep us informed and to keep us feeling concerned about our fellow citizens. Likewise, in regions of the country such as northern Ontario, which represents 88 per cent of the land mass, we have two broadcasting studios: one in Sudbury and one in Thunder Bay.
Surprisingly CBC radio, which has covered most of northern Ontario only for the past few years, does a tremendous job of keeping us informed even in the regions. The area is so vast that its role is really very well carried out. It keeps us advised. If you live in Sudbury you do not hear much about Sault Ste. Marie except
through CBC radio; likewise across the entire north. I think CBC radio does a tremendous service.
Another area I want to touch on relates to the cuts in CBC. This government, in its wisdom or lack of wisdom, has cut CBC's budget by some $240 million since 1984. This is really shameful when we look at its national unity role, the role to inform Canadians. CBC radio has a special role for one area of our country which is perhaps more important than any other, and that is its role in rural Canada.
Rural Canada is suffering in every sector of the country, but in no area of public life does CBC play a more important role than in agriculture because it is so diverse. We do not have one country when it comes to agriculture; we have about five. One important role that CBC Radio has carried through the years was the agriculture and resources representative on Parliament Hill.
It was done for many years by George Price. It was a terribly ungracious way that CBC advised him that he was not only being retired, but that his position was being dumped.
The agriculture committee of the House of Commons fought that decision. We got some commitments that the service would be continued. It has not. The government has failed-

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROTECTION FOR WHISTLE BLOWERS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROTECTION FOR WHISTLE BLOWERS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider providing legislated protection to all environmental "whistle-blowers".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity today to speak on M-149, which is a motion
November 29, 1990

in my name, asking that the House and the government consider providing legislative protection for whistle blowing.
For many who are listening and watching, they probably do not know what such a motion is about. I would hope after I have covered the waterfront for 20 minutes, they will have a better idea of why it is so important that this Parliament and this country have whistle blowing legislation.
It is just as important as access to information or as having an environmental auditor. Without whistle blowing legislation, we will continue to see an awful lot of environmental offences continue without being reported to the appropriate authorities or being made public.
The intention of whistle blowing legislation is to protect the whistle blower, those who either phone the RCMP, Environment Canada or a local newspaper, or who make an environmental problem public.
It is to protect the environment and taxpayers from crime, losses from crime, criminal activity, and illegal and improper activities related to the environment. It is desperately needed not only to protect those workers, both public and private sector, but it is needed to protect the environment.
Many people fear job loss should they blow the whistle on their employer. They fear pay cuts, law suits, harassment and intimidation for reporting either on their industry or employer, even if they are just a member of the general public reporting on an environmental problem that they see occurring in, around or near their community.
The purpose of the legislation would be to encourage those who witness or are aware of illegal activity that significantly impairs the environment to report it and make it public. I am glad to see the minister of health listening to this most interesting debate, because he would know that within the medical and health field, whistle blowing is practically built within the system.
If there are problems with drugs or a certain kind of health care, the whistle is blown on them internally within the medical or health care system so that those problems can be dealt with quickly prior to the health or welfare of individuals who might be in the hospital or in the health care system being negatively impacted.
Private Members' Business
However, in the years that I have served in this House, I have witnessed many public and private sector whistle blowers who had been singled out and punished. I suppose more members of the opposition receive brown envelopes than do government members. Quite often, I find members of the opposition, including myself, know of things before some ministers do. That seems to be the nature of some kinds of negative policy decisions, that the opposition is made aware of them quickly, before they can be implemented.
Those who are punished, particularly those where there is a negative political impact or where the corporate masters are embarrassed or forced to clean up, quite often the political or corporate master will take some kind of singling out or punishment against those who have reported.
I have attended many meetings with trade unionists in recent months and years. For example just two weeks ago I attended the Canadian Labour Congress environment conference in Edmonton where there was extensive consideration for the need for whistle blowing legislation. Workers who witnessed, for example, spills at pulp mills, either intentional or accidental, at nuclear facilities, whether it was intention or accidental, or at other industrial sites, have found that many of their co-workers from the shop floor who have reported illegal activities that they have seen, or accidents that could endanger the environment, are singled out or red circled, or other kinds of punitive action are taken against them by their employers. There is a widespread fear for an individual's job when he or she reports on offences. Despite that, many trade unions are setting up special committees that go ahead and whistle blow anyway.
Offences that are criminal, for example, where the teller in a bank reports on a robbery, generally the manager or someone else within the banking system lauds that kind of whistle blowing. Quite often they are given a raise in pay and are seen as heroes in the community. The recent wave of white collar crime that we have seen both here and in the United States indicates how much stronger the whistle blowing legislation hotline tip system needs to be if we are to root out the degree of white collar crime that has been unleashed upon us within financial institutions and in other areas of our society.

Private Members' Business
Whistle blowing legislation is necessary to turn around the prevailing fear of punishment in order to make whistle blowing a right and respected duty. In some cases, it should provide for fine splitting, something we find in some areas of federal legislation already. There needs to be that kind of encouragement in areas where there are particularly nasty forms of environmental degradation going on. Where the courts ultimately bring a fine against those who have been perpetrating the offence, the fine should be split with those who have been involved with blowing the whistle.
Whistle blowing legislation is necessary to halt environmental degradation. I recall the former Liberal Minister of the Environment in this province of Ontario who, after there had been 13 spills in a one-week period on the St. Clair River, described that as industrial incontinence but did not proceed to lay charges or to levy the kinds of fines that would be necessary to stop that kind of industrial incontinence.
I recall the former federal Minister of the Environment telling me that some 80 per cent of the toxic and hazardous waste produced on a daily basis in this country is improperly or illegally disposed of. It is dumped in rivers, dumped in sewers, dumped on farmers fields and it requires whistle blowing legislation to start getting these kinds of activities reported so that kind of future problem can be disposed of before it occurs. I see the minister of forests is here. He is a big supporter of whistle blowing legislation. I hope he takes it to cabinet this week and we see it back here fairly soon.
In the forestry sector, we need some whistle blowing, mostly whistle blowing about what the minister is not doing. I recall that Dr. Rankin from the University of Victoria Law School did an assessment and an evaluation of class one and class two waste management permits in British Columbia last year. He found that fully, three-quarters of the waste management permits in some areas of the province in some categories had been in significant non-compliance for more than a year.
At the federal level, we found from the Auditor General that there has been a 240 per cent increase in non-compliance among mining companies, as an example, since the Conservatives came to office. I do not think the government understands how strongly Canadians feel about protecting the environment and stopping that kind of improper use of our environment.
The Auditor General found that most of the mines audited in this country were non-compliance with the federal legislation that they were operating under. The majority of the mines or workers at all or most of these sites know that there is improper activity going on. The drivers of the trucks that are hauling and dumping toxic waste out into some farmer's field in British Columbia or in Prince Edward Island tonight know what they are doing. The environment is being destroyed in many areas of Canada by what is described as insignificant increment; a spill here, a dump there, a fire here, some radiation there, an oil spill here and some acid mine drainage there. Whistle blowers legislation to encourage and protect workers and citizens for reporting environmental accidents and hazards is a fundamental piece of legislation that must be passed by this House.
It is federal policy within the NDP. It is the only party that has the kind of process to set policy prior to getting into government. I certainly hope and expect that we will have a chance to perhaps bring in this kind of legislation. If the Green Plan had any real guts-I suppose we may not see the Green Plan now in 1990 according to the latest rumours around here-but if it had any real guts, whistle blowing legislation would be a centrepiece, just as an environmental auditor general would be a centrepiece, and major amendments to access to information and environmental liaison centres would be similar centrepieces in the legislation.
The chances are low. The reason I say that is we can measure it under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, which is the direct responsibility of the present Minister of the Environment. The Auditor General found that since the legislation became law more than two years ago, there have only been three prosecutions in the whole of Canada, three prosecutions and three convictions under the most important and broadest based environmental legislation in the whole country. The prevailing philosophy of this government in a big business is that the environment is free, and one externalizes waste to increase one's profit.

There is no Green Plan either coming or existing under the Tories in my view. What we are seeing is an environmental and ecological brown-out. We are seeing immunity from prosecution, Order in Council exemptions for special friends, such as the Alcan Kemano II project in British Columbia, special laws on liability, such as the ones put in place for the Atomic Energy Control Board. Let me give a direct example on the government's mythical war on pollution and protection of the environment.
There was a discretionary immunity memo leaked some time ago that I made public. We know now that fisheries contamination from industrial pollution and toxins from B.C. pulp mills is far worse than ever expected. On the front page of today's Vancouver Sun the headline is, "Six mill areas cited. Dioxins spark expanded bans". We see that areas as much as five times the size of the area already closed have been restricted. Affected are the waters around the Fletcher Challenge's Crofton mill near Duncan, the Fletcher Challenge mill near Campbell River, the MacMillan Bloedel mill at Power River on the Sunshine Coast, the MacMillan Bloedel mill near Nanaimo, the Canadian Forest Products mill near Gold River and the Eurocan mill near Kitimat.
Already 1 per cent of the fisheries in British Columbia are closed because of environmental pollution from pulp mills. That is shellfish, it is crab, prawn, shrimps and now it is starting to move into the fish populations. It is truly incredible. The question of compensation for fishermen has not been addressed. The prosecution of companies and agencies involved has not been addressed. The matter of ruined native fisheries has not been addressed and matter of public health has not been addressed.
The only reason the government finally acted on November 23, 1989 was because a former federal public servant by the name of Otto Langer wrote a memo of November 15, 1989 which outlined the inconsistent application of the Fisheries Act, which was leaked to the press, embarrassed the government into taking some action, band-aid actions, after the fact actions, too little too late action, but with whistle blowing legislation the public would not have to wait for a situation to reach crisis proportions economically, ecologically and environmentally and then hope that someone leaks the information to trigger a response.
Private Members' Business
On the inconsistent application of the Fisheries Act as a case in point, I am not talking about a rare isolated example. What Mr. Langer revealed is that the issue is one of continuous non-compliance, for example, involving 19 years of the Department of the Environment environmental protection never charging anyone despite the knowledge that the pulp mills were totally out of compliance with the pulp and paper effluent regulations. It is an issue of chronic non-compliance. "Senior management and conservative legal opinion has recently created new classes of immunity for certain polluters or those that destroy habitat". This led to examples of abandoning court cases when clear "others beyond our influence did not want the trials to continue". In other words, forget prosecuting the big polluters.
The leaked memo continues on the top of page 4 and I quote again:
The impact of creating the above classes of immunity have far reaching consequences for the morale of our staff and ultimately the future of the fishery resource and associated environment-A continuation of this philosophy will result in a wholesale loss of fish habitat and a continued degradation of water quality.
If repeated violators are not being dealt with, what kind of an environment are we going to be left with? Just yesterday in The Toronto Star there was a very good article called "The Mythical War on Pollution" which said the following:
-since 1970, Ottawa's enforcement of federal environmental laws has ranged from timid to non-existent.
The evidence of that 20-year regulatory failure is overwhelming. Internal Environment Canada reports and memos confirm that many of Canada's worst polluters in 1970 are still the worst today.
Among the most notorious are Canada's pulp and paper mills. Almost half are still breaking the Fisheries Act regulations each day they operate.
I am blowing the whistle today but is the minister of fisheries going to go out and charge any of these hundreds of polluters who are violating federal law? Well, we will find out tomorrow morning but you and I both know the answer, Mr. Speaker. This government is granting immunity to prosecution to hundreds of corporations in this country who are breaking the law at this very moment.
The article goes on:

November 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
From 1985 through 1988, the average Fisheries Act fine was $4,100. Only 56 convictions were registered during those 48 months and a minority of the prosecutions were initiated by Environment Canada. What happened to the public policy?
The paper goes on to conclude that there is an interim immunity from prosecution.
Each secret deal Ottawa made with these companies triggered demands from competitors that they get the same break.
This pattern is reflected in a Statistics Canada analysis of capital expenditures by Canadian manufacturers between 1985 and 1989. Of a total capital investment of $25 billion, 96 per cent was spent on expansion and modernization. A mere 2 per cent was spent directly on pollution abatement and most of that money was federal and provincial anti-pollution grants.
That is a pretty telling story about what is going on and what is not going on.
Let us look now for a moment at what the Auditor General has found. I think I can demonstrate why workers want it, why the public wants it, why the environment deserves it, why federal public servants need it, and why we need to stop companies from breaking the law.
In 1984 and 1985 he looked at 13 departments and in 1985 he reported it to the President of the Treasury Board. In February, 1987, the President of the Treasury Board sent out a policy circular called "Losses of Money Suffered by Her Majesty and Offences and other Illegal Acts against the Crown".
In 1988 the Auditor General took another look and this is what he said that most of the six departments examined had not established the procedures required by Treasury Board for reporting all suspected cases of fraud and other offences to the RCMP, the deputy attorney general and the Treasury Board and for reporting all proven cases to Parliament.
I quote from section 19.10:
We are concerned about the tendency by some departments to not always report cases to the RCMP.
Well, what is going on, Mr. Speaker? Illegal activity is found in 13 departments by the Auditor General. He goes to the President of the Treasury Board, who then circulates it. Five years later the Auditor General goes back and looks at half those departments again and finds the illegal activity is still going on and it is not being reported to the RCMP.
Obviously we need whistle-blowing legislation. My colleagues in British Columbia have introduced a bill to protect no-pollution informants. It is Bill M 208.
Let us take a look at the evidence of the Auditor General again when he appeared on December 12 of last year before the public accounts committee in his discussions about the need for a hot line. On the hotline idea, he said: "The first principle it needs to clear is that the government bears the primary responsibility for preventing and detecting waste, mismanagement, and fraud in government, not my office".
That is the auditor general. He said they audited the government's fraud reporting practices in 1984. "We reported serious deficiencies. Departments continue to express concerns that individuals would be reluctant to report for fear of reprisal".
Mr. Speaker, my legislation is a proposed way to protect those individuals who fear reprisals for reporting to the RCMP. I go on and quote:

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate and to follow my esteemed colleague, the hon. member for Skeena, who has once again given evidence as to why he has a widely recognized expertise in chronic effluent. I am pleased to speak on this motion, proposed by the member for Skeena. The motion states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider
providing legislated protection to all environmental "whistleblowers".
I would like to start by reminding my hon. colleagues that the government has, in fact, seen fit to provide such protection under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. The matter was discussed before this House. Members of the committee that was struck to carry out the clause-by-clause review of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, then known as Bill C-74, heard submissions and arguments both for and against this point. It is obviously an issue about which there are different points of view, and there was debate before the committee. There was also debate on other clauses of the bill designed to encourage public participation in enforcement of federal environmental statutes.
For example, the clause which gave the right to individuals to oblige the minister to investigate alleged violations of the act did, in fact, give rise to considerable debate for and against the question. Some briefs showed a fear of increased public participation. They were against giving individuals the right to require the Minister of the Environment to investigate alleged offences under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act as well as the right to receive a report of the investigation.
Private Members' Business
Some briefs did not support whistle blower protection and others wanted such protection, across the board, for every offence under the proposed act. Some of those who opposed further public participation in the implementation and enforcement of federal environmental law believed that the government was running the risk of creating a highly politicized climate of confrontation which, in fact, could jeopardize the pursuit of environmental objectives. Others saw the public participation and public rights sections of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act as devices for ensuring the public's help in enforcement and for reinforcing the public's belief that the government was committed to protecting the environment.
The House of Commons, doing clause-by-clause review of Bill C-74, decided to promote further public participation. This review reduced the number of individuals who may require the Minister of the Environment to investigate alleged offences against the proposed Canadian Environmental Protection Act from 12 down to two. Section 108, Section 109, and Section 110 of the act outline the requirements.
108.	(1) Any two persons resident in Canada who are not less than 18 years of age and who are of the opinion that an offence has been committed under this act may apply to the minister for an investigation of the alleged offence.
(2)	An application for an investigation shall be accompanied by a solemn or statutory declaration.
A)	Stating the names and addresses of the applicants;
B)	Stating the nature of the alleged offence and the name of each person alleged to be involved in its commission; and
C)	Containing a concise statement of the evidence supporting the allegations of the applicants.
Section 109 goes on to continue to spell out these requirements:
109.	(1) On receipt of an application under Section 108, the minister shall acknowledge receipt of the application and investigate all matters that the minister considers necessary for a determination of the facts relating to the alleged offence.
Clearly this is designed to ensure that the minister has in his or her hands all of the facts relating to the case. It continues:
(2) Within ninety days after receiving an application under Section 108, the minister shall report to the applicants on the progress of the investigation and the action, if any, that the minister proposes to take.

Private Members' Business
(3)	The minister may discontinue an investigation where the minister is of the opinion that the alleged offence does not require further investigation.
(4)	Where an investigation is discontinued, the minister shall
A)	Prepare a report in writing describing the information obtained during the investigation and stating the reasons for its discontinuation; and
B)	Send a copy of the report to the applicants and to any person whose conduct was investigated.
110.	At any stage of an investigation under Section 109, the minister may, in addition to or in lieu of continuing the investigation, send any records, returns or evidence to the Attorney General of Canada for consideration of whether an offence has been or is about to be committed against this act and for such action as the Attorney General of Canada may wish to take.
In addition, it also decided in favour of experimental so-called whistle blower protection. The committee limited the right of individuals to request anonymity solely when they report the unauthorized release of a regulated substance under Part II of the act governing toxic substances, or a release of regulated emissions, effluents and wastes under Part IV of the act governing federal departments, agencies, commissions, boards, works, undertakings, as well as federal lands and federal Crown corporations.
Accordingly, in Part II of the act governing toxic substances, section 37 requires that an individual who has knowledge of an authorized release or of the likelihood of an unauthorized release must report this information to a designated inspector or to any other person designated by regulation as empowered to receive the report.
That section also provides for voluntary reports from individuals who are not required under law to transmit their information but who in the interests of environmental protection may choose to do so. A person not required to report may request that his or her identity remain confidential. Once an individual makes this request, no person may release or cause to be released the identity of the informant or any information or detail likely to reveal that identity. I quote:
37. (1) Where a person has knowledge of the occurrence or reasonable likelihood of a release into the environment of a substance specified in the list of toxic substances in Schedule I, but the person is not required to report the matter under this act, the person may report any information relating to the release or likely release to an inspector or to any person to whom a report may be made under Section 36.
I believe that my time is close to expiring. I will simply wrap up by saying that I am sure over time the government will consider many types of measures. One of those might be the extension of whistle blower provisions. If this is studied, I am sure the government will find the most appropriate way of using such protection, keeping in mind, of course, the rights of the accused and other important factors.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak out in favour of this motion. Canadians are becoming increasingly serious about their responsibility for the environment, both as individuals and as employees.

If we truly want to create a system where every individual can be a guardian of the environment, the kind of legislation proposed in the motion is absolutely essential. Individuals want to take responsibility in the workplace as well as in their personal lives. Fortunately, more and more businesses are also recognizing the importance of being guardians of the environment and are recognizing that doing things in an environmentally friendly way also makes good sense economically and for their increased productivity and efficiency as businesses.
Others are putting their heads in the sand, pretending that this concern about the environment is a new thing and it is going to go away, if only they ignore it. Sooner or later, the world will get back to more important things and leave them alone to pollute our air, water and soil.
However, that is not what is going to happen because people are fundamentally realizing that the environmental problems they face now are a question of their own personal health and safety, that if we do not act urgently on such problems as ozone depletion and global warming, we will not have air to breathe and we will not have clean water to drink, and that the time horizon for that is sooner, rather than later. So people do want to take their individual responsibility very seriously.
They know that in their place of work perhaps effluents are being put into rivers, lakes and oceans, damaging the ability of life on earth to survive in the future. They know that chemicals are being used and not disposed of safely. They know that their own personal health and safety as employees is at risk in their

workplace. They want to protect that, but just as important, they want to protect the environment that they are going to leave to their children.
The hon. member opposite who was speaking quoted the provisions in the current legislation. One of the things I noticed is that it obliges reporting on behalf of individuals who are aware of existing pollution or potential pollution, but it provides no protection.
It is much more than a question of simply keeping confidential the identity of an individual who has made a complaint or made a report. It requires a very positive legislative provision which protects that individual from retaliation, and gives them a complete mechanism if they have been retaliated against. That ensures that they, in their interest to do a public duty in protecting the environment by lodging a complaint, will not suffer the loss of their job, lose employment opportunities or suffer the retribution and wrath of their employer.
We have to take this motion seriously because the ability of government to enforce environmental legislation is limited by the resources available, by the number of people who can be hired by a government at any particular time to go into virtually every small factory, shop and plant in this country, and determine how environmentally sound their practices are. I do not think any of us want to see a situation where only through an army of inspectors and enforcers can we achieve a cleaner and safer world.
The cost of that would be horrendous. But the cost of not dealing with this problem is also horrendous. I go back to one particular experience when I was on municipal council. It had to do with a very small amount of copper sulphate spread on the parking lot of a high technology company in the west end of this region. That is a standard way of disposing of some chemicals for some companies. It leaked into the water and literally put out of commission for many days the sewage treatment plant so that for close to a week raw sewage was going into the Ottawa River, simply because of one careless act by one careless business, and at a public cost for those few days of $3 million dollars to put that sewage treatment plant back into condition.
Private Members' Business
If we want to avoid these things without a massive bureaucracy that will go into every workplace across Canada, the best way to do it is to give the people working in those plants with those employers the ability to draw attention to problems that occur so that they can be dealt with and solved before they create this kind of horrendous damage and public expense.
Many employers are starting to realize this and are putting into place a mechanism whereby their employees are free to bring these problems or suggestions to the attention of management or suggestions as to how they could use less resources to dispose of waste more safely and generally create a more environmentally friendly workplace and a more environmentally friendly corporate citizen. However, many other companies are not doing that. Employees who dared to make a report or to talk to a senior manager about damaging practices would lose their job and benefits very quickly. People are not prepared to fulfil their social responsibility if that is the cost. If it is a social responsibility, it is a social obligation to protect them when they fulfil that duty.
I have seen what happens to people when they come forward and complain of wrongdoing in their place of employment, whether it is theft by other employees or whether it is fairly rampant fraud within an employment situation. Despite the best will at the political level to protect them and to protect their jobs once they return to their work unit, other forces take over and it becomes impossible to protect them, except through legislation.
We see this happen when there are complaints, even in the Public Service, possibly and particularly in the Public Service when there are complaints of violations of human rights or complaints of harassment. We still have not put in place a system whereby somebody can make that kind of complaint against systemic discrimination and have it dealt with without suffering the consequences of having made a complaint.
I have known and I continue to hear from people who are without a job because they dared to complain against their employer. I met with one as recently as this morning. I have met with people who have taken up to 10 years to get justice against a complaint of harassment, sexual, racial or religious.

Private Members' Business
We cannot allow that to happen in the environmental area. We cannot allow people who are trying to carry out a responsibility to society and to the future of the world to be punished for it.
Within the Public Service generally there has been a call for a long time for whistle blowing and, as my hon. colleague who introduced the motion said, the support of the Auditor General is very strong for a system that would allow employees to bring to the attention of management, or of politicians, complaints about theft from government, fraud in government, complaints about anything that is not being done according to government policy and is being done to the detriment of the public. I think that is good legislation.
We want to create responsible, independent thinkers in our public service and in the private sector, but in our public service particularly because we are the largest employer in the country. We want to make it not only a right but a responsibility of every employee to take their environmental responsibility seriously without fear of retaliation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion proposed by my colleague, "That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider providing legislated protection to all environmental 'whistle-blowers'," is a most interesting proposition.
I am very pleased to make some comments on this matter. Whistle blower protection provisions to protect the identity of informants of suspected or apparent violations are fairly new in federal legislation. At least three federal statutes provide limited protection to individuals who bring complaints or participate in proceedings or other enforcement activities. These are the Labour Code, the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
In the Canada Labour Code, employees are protected from employers engaging in unfair practices such as harassment, firing or suspension when employees exercise their rights under the code. For example, to lay a complaint, disclose information about employer violations of the code, or testifying or otherwise participating in proceedings under the code. If the Canada Labour Code board judges that unfair practices have indeed taken place, the board can make corrective orders or direct that compensation be paid. The protection is limited, however, to employers' unfair practices and does not extend to concealing the employer's identity at his or her request.
One section of the labour code that does allow an employer's identity to remain undisclosed is clause 146 (4) of the code. It provides that a person who provides information to a safety officer in relation to inspections will have his or her identity concealed. Disclosure is not compellable before any court or other tribunal. Violations of section 146 are punishable on summary conviction.
I quote clause 146.(4):
No person to whom information obtained pursuant to section 144 is communicated in confidence
a)	shall divulge the name of the informant to any person, except for the purposes of this part; or
b)	in competent or compellable to divulge the name of the informant before any court or other tribunal.
There is additional protection as well. The Canadian Human Rights Act, for example, provides in section 59 that no person shall threaten, intimidate or discriminate against an individual because he or she made a complaint, gave evidence or assisted in any way in a proceeding under the act. The penalty for contravention of this section by an employer is a fine of up to $50,000, and for any other party, a fine of up to $5,000.
Again, I quote from section 59 of the act:
No person shall threaten, intimidate or discriminate against an individual because that individual has made a complaint or given evidence or assisted in any way in respect of the initiation or prosecution of a complaint or other proceeding under this part, or because that individual proposes to do so.
Also, there is the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. It is unique among federal environmental statutes in that it provides the right to request anonymity for those who provide information to enforcement authorities in certain situation. These circumstances are limited to reports of an unauthorized release or of a likely release of a toxic substance to the environment, where the individual is not legally bound by the statute to make a report and does so voluntarily.

November 29, 1990

There are similar provisions for persons reporting unauthorized releases of effluents, emissions or wastes by federal departments, boards, commissions, agencies, federal Crown corporations and federal works or undertakings on federal lands. If the informant is an employee of the federal entity, there is an added benefit. The employee making the report cannot be disciplined, dismissed or harassed for having done so.
More specifically, subsections 37 (2) and (3) and 58 (2) and (3), provide that there a person making such a report requests to remain anonymous, his or her identity shall not be released unless he or she authorizes the release in writing. Subsections 37 (4) and 58 (4) provide that no employee shall be disciplined, dismissed or harassed for making a report to a CEPA inspector.
It is fair to say that most managers would certainly prefer to learn about a release of a toxic substance at their facility from an employee rather than from a visiting CEPA inspector. For this reason, managers are advised to encourage their staff to report to them any release or suspected release or conditions that are likely to result in release.
The government is satisfied with the operation of these existing provisions. While extending the current protection to all environmental whistle blowers may seem attractive in some cases, there are important considerations to ponder.
For example, when my colleague refers to protection for all environmental whistle blowers in his motion, I wonder if he means all informants who report alleged environmental offences. Under the Constitution Act, 1982, the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over local works and undertakings, except for navigation, railways, canals, telecommunication companies, broadcasters, banks, aircraft, airports, commercial air services, interprovincial ferries, trucking and other transport. All other works come under provincial jurisdiction. This is repeated in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
Since provinces have jurisdiction, it is provincial law which governs the right of employees in the work place. We have a practical problem here, because to legislate this protection for matters that are dealt with in provincial law would require intensive study by the Department of Justice to determine even if such a thing was constitutionally possible.
Private Members' Business
In addition, decisions of Canada's high courts are tending to erode some of the previous traditional claims to protection of personal identity made by informants of criminal offences. The courts must weigh the right of the accused to face his or her accuser against the benefits of receiving tips or other evidence of criminal offences that enforcement agencies may not otherwise have been able to receive.
While more than one community has pointed to the success afforded by Crime Stoppers or other programs where informants are paid for information leading to successful convictions and guaranteed that their identity will be protected, it is true that a person who reports a Criminal Code offence under the Crime Stoppers program still has no legislated protection under that program against harassment or loss of employment, if he or she has made a complaint against an employer or against a fellow worker.
There appears to be a growing trend, however, in other jurisdictions such as British Columbia and the United States to look more extensively at whistle blower protection, but there are problems with this. In their paper for the recent book, Law Reform for Sustainable Development in British Columbia, two lawyers published a short discussion of the problem of whistle blower protection in British Columbia for reports of suspected or apparent environmental violations. They defined whistle blowers as employees who disclose employer violations of environmental laws to their management, union, government, or the media.
The authors of this paper note that given current resources for law enforcement employees can be an adjunct of enforcement, but it is important to note that this can happen only if they report offences without jeopardizing their livelihood. The authors do not deal, however, with the protection of identity but with legislative provisions that would protect any employee's entitlement to his or her job. There is also the argument that there is a possibility of whistle blowing legislation being used as a means to harass employers by disgruntled employees.
Whistle blower provisions in statutes of various provinces seem to lean more toward job protection than protection of an informant's identity. The statutes of other countries such as the United States and court decisions related to the interpretation of these statutes

Private Members' Business
are interesting. We must study all these things very carefully and very soberly.
We would certainly agree that my colleague has brought to the government some food for future thought.
