Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that this follow-up to an earlier question should follow this debate on environmental issues. That, of course, is at the heart of the question which I wish to follow up.
In April of this past year, a cross river barge project was established in the city of Windsor against the objections the various downriver communities in the area, which make up part of my constituency.
In a series of questions with the government, I raised the possibility of what I consider to be the necessity of an environmental assessment review proceeding taking place with respect to this new barge, because this barge service was not just a service to provide transportation across the river. It was specifically a service designed to take dangerous goods from one side of the Detroit River to the other. It was to be devoted exclusively to such dangerous goods.
Since the question was originally raised in a series of questions in January, April and May of 1990, we have been able to get access under Access to Information to the file which is kept in the Department of Transport with respect to this project.
On the basis of the material in that file, which has been released to us, I have to make a number of charges with respect to the government's treatment of this whole question.
First, I charge that this government deliberately covered up the fact that this barge project was proceeding forward and was being given considerable attention by various departments of government, was of considerable importance and was recognized to be of such by the people of the city of Windsor and the downriver communities. Yet at no stage did the government of this country see fit to tell the people of Windsor and Essex county that this barge proposal was being revived.
Despite the fact that in the information which has been provided to us under Access to Information there were September 1989 meetings which took place specifically on the issue. It was reported that this barge proposal had been revived and was being considered in detailed meetings at the very highest levels within ministries here in Ottawa.
Yet, as I say, at no time was any information on this subject provided to the people of the city of Windsor and the county of Essex.
I raised a question in the House on January 26, 1990 with the Minister of Transport about this subject. The Minister of Transport, at that stage, said to me that this was simply a possibility. He said to me that the question was premature. This despite the fact the files now show that this government and the minister's own department had been for a period of at least four months considering in detail the question of whether this barge should go forward.
I also have to say that the file shows quite clearly that the government suppressed information with respect to barge operations on the Detroit River. In particular, they refused to tell people in our community that there had been seven accidents in the previous period of less than seven years with respect to other barge operations taking place, barge operations that did not exclusively handle dangerous goods.
I also have to charge on the basis of the files which I have seen that the government did not at any stage undertake a serious environmental review of this barge proposal. This is despite the fact that the Minister of National Revenue stood up in the House and said that such a serious review would take place.
I raised this question on May 7, 1990 with the Minister of the Environment asking him why the government, despite concerns expressed by the community, had rejected public environmental assessment hearings on this Windsor barge. The minister did not respond to the question and did not provide us with any justification for the cover-up and the suppression of information, which had clearly taken place with respect to this question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is familiar with the proposal made by Barge Transport Incorporated of Detroit, which plans to load tanker trucks carrying hazardous sub-

Adjournment Debate
stances on barges, to cross the Detroit River in the Windsor area. An initial plan was examined in 1987. If the company had followed through, the plan would have been subject to the environmental assessment review process, since it concerned federal land.
However, the company withdrew its initial plan and, after considering other possibilities, has now proposed another plan that does not involve federal land. Nevertheless, because of concerns raised by members of the local community, a thorough review was made of the new plan to determine, without going through the environmental assessment review process, whether any federal requirements or regulations applied. After wide-ranging consultations by senior officials from various federal departments, it was concluded that the plan was well within all regulatory and other requirements concerning health, safety and transportation of hazardous materials as defined by the Canadian Coast Guard, which is responsible for ships' safety. The federal government will carry out inspections and a take samples as required, to ensure compliance with the emergency order on imports and exports of contaminated fuel, issued under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the CEPA regulations on imports and exports of hazardous wastes are expected to come into force by early 1991. They will authorize the federal government to control future imports and exports of hazardous wastes.
From the risk point of view, the planned barge transport compares with the way in which any other product, like oil, for instance, is shipped on the Great Lakes. At the present time, a number of companies are transporting hazardous materials by barge in international waters, and they have excellent safety standards.
This plan offers an effective alternative to transportation over land. It helps reduce truck traffic on the Bluewater Bridge in Sarnia and in surrounding communities like Wallaceburg and Chatham.
The crossing by ferryboat would replace road transportation on roughly 400 km, reducing the risk of road accidents, hence spillage of dangerous goods.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise once again on a question I asked the Minister of National Revenue on November 8.
The question concerned veterans and other Canadians who have been told that a beeper which summons emergency health services does not fall under medical devices in the goods and services tax schedule. This would make it tax exempt if it did so.
The Department of Veterans Affairs must consider this instrument to be an essential service as it pays for the device under the Blue Cross. I asked the minister for his justification of taxing such a device which can mean the difference between life and death. The answer was rather confusing. He said that the Royal Canadian Legion is considered to be a charitable organization for the purposes of GST and therefore would not be obligated to pay or to collect the GST. This did not, in any way, answer the question. I was concerned with a device that is used by veterans and many other Canadians, and which is not distributed through the Royal Canadian Legion. Perhaps the minister was not listening and thought I was requiring about something else. I cannot be sure.
I rise today hoping to get a response and at this time I hope the response is pertinent to the issue. Following my question, I wrote a letter to the minister regarding the Health Line beeper. At this time I would like to briefly outline the contents of the letter to provide the House with some background on this very worth-while life-saving device.
The Health Line beeper is a portable device which allows the user to summon emergency health services by tapping the device. The message is relayed to a 24-hour monitoring centre and services are dispatched. This service is used primarily by elderly and/or chronically ill persons.
A constituent of mine, Cathy Collard, is the manager of Health Line Services in Charlottetown. She inquired whether the device would be tax exempt under the proposed goods and services tax. On her behalf I contacted officials within the minister's department who stated that since the device is not listed under "medical devices" in the goods and services tax schedule, it would not be tax exempt.

Adjournment Debate
For chronically ill and elderly people, the possession of a Health Line beeper could mean the difference between life and death. I would like to stress that it is not a luxury item and I fail to understand why it is not considered a medical device for the purposes of taxation.
The personal emergency beeper is needed most by those who may live alone or who are left alone during the day. This service, without any argument, can be a life-saving service. It allows one to cope alone and with dignity despite age or illness. With one simple push of a button in a moment of need, the urgently needed assistance is on its way.
I am appalled that this government could even consider not making such a device tax exempt. Is this government so cold that it will not listen to Canadians for any reason, proving how insensitive it is to the concerns of Canadians. All I am asking is that a device that quite often means the difference between life and death be tax exempt.
At this time we are going through a full-blown, made-in-Canada recession. Everywhere you turn people are feeling the crunch. This is a time when we must help those people who need us most. I am referring to those people who need and deserve their independence and without an emergency beeper would not be able to do so.
I must stress that this government must start listening to the concerns of all Canadians and help those in need. It is time that this government began to realize that a price cannot be placed on human life. At this time, I would like to stress that I am quite aware that under certain circumstances devices such as this will in fact be considered as medical devices and, therefore, will be zero rated for the purpose of GST. However, as I checked into the matter with officials from the departments of Finance and National Revenue, as well as the GST hotline, I was told repeatedly that the health line beeper does not fall under that category.
I am also aware that communication devices, other than a device for use with telegraph or telephone apparatus, will be zero rated when specifically designed to assist an individual in coping with or treating an illness or chronic abnormal physical state. I must point out once
again that I have been told by GST officials that this health beeper does not fall under this category.
I ask the parliamentary secretary tonight and hopefully he will do everything in his power to ensure that this device will be given all consideration and that it should be tax exempt.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague went through his question dated November 8, 1990, on page 15327 of Hansard where the minister answered his question. He said today that he was pleased that he was advised, but he did not mention that this government took its responsibility and the minister answered his letter which he had today.
I refer him to the second paragraph where the minister said: "I am pleased to advise you that in certain circumstances these devices will in fact be considered as medical devices and therefore will be zero rated for the purpose of the GST", which my hon. friend mentioned, but he did not say it was from the letter of the minister.

So, Mr. Speaker, I will go on. I wish to answer in greater detail to the question raised by the hon. member for Hillsborough on the exemption from the proposed Goods and Services Thx, of beepers used to communicate with emergency services.
Even without any additional information on the use of the devices the hon. member is referring to, I am quite sure these communication devices will be exempted. In some cases, the devices will be exempted for GST purposes, as the minister indicated in his letter.
The regulations established by the Department of Finance stipulates the conditions under which such communication devices, used for medical purposes, can be exempted from the GST. For example, communication devices, other than those used with phones and telegraph apparatus, will be exempted if they are specially designed to help sick or chronically-ill people. Consequently, beepers designed for this purpose will be GST-free. Moreover, breathing apparatus which can be used at home will also be exempted if especially designed to help the sick or the chronically-ill. It should be noted that beepers designed for use with telephones or telegraphs will be taxable.

Our government is committed to make health care readily accessible to all Canadians. To that end we have granted generous tax rebates on medical services, prescription drugs and medical devices. Under the proposed legislation most medical services will be tax exempt. This category also includes products or services whose cost is paid or reimbursed by a provincial government pursuant to a plan established through provincial legislation for the supply of health care services to all provincial residents covered under that insurance.
The tax on prescription drugs and medical devices will be removed. The prescription drugs listed in the various annexes of the Food and Drugs Act, the Food and Drugs Regulations and the Narcotic Control Act, other than drugs available without prescription, will no longer be taxable. The legislation provides that some medical devices will not be taxable if they are prescribed by a physician.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I return once again to a subject I have raised numerous times in this House and which I raised on November 20 as a question to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. It has to do with the Scotia Synfuels Project, the project to create a refinery or converting a new technology for making petroleum distillates out of coal and heavy oil in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia.
It is a project which has widespread support in the region. It is a major economic development project for Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia. It is ideally suited for the economy of the area, particularly in the fact that it finds a clean use for Cape Breton coal which is known to be of a high sulphur content and therefore difficult to use, particularly because of the hydrocarbons it emits.
The Scotia Synfuels Project is a technology which has been in development for many years and is at a point now where it is nearly commercially viable and would be commercially viable with the assistance that is normally available through this federal government's programs had the Department of Industry Science and Technology, and particularly the minister, seen fit to exercise a little
Adjournment Debate
bit of creativity and take a risk on a project that is ideal for our region.
I must say the people of eastern Nova Scotia still cannot believe that the minister, after all the noises that have been made by the government, turned down their request for tax credits.
The reasons stated by the minister on November 20 for turning down the application for tax credits under the Cape Breton tax credit program were as he said in the House. What the promoters of the project requested was first that they wanted to have a $200 million Cape Breton tax credit. They wanted to have more. They also wanted to have a loan guarantee and an interest buy-down. That was not possible because of the fact there was no private sector money guarantee.
This is precisely the point. What the promoters had been asking the federal government for years, and particularly during the period of time when they had put in for the Cape Breton tax credit, was an indication from the federal government that if the tax credit would be forthcoming, they would be going on the private money markets to obtain the private sector funding that would be forthcoming, they believed, under current product prices for the petroleum products they were going to produce.
Therefore, what was being asked for by the company was simply an assurance by the federal government that those moneys would be available so that they could go out and get the private sector money. Unfortunately, this government was unwilling to even give them that undertaking and aborted the project in midstream.
What the minister is saying is not correct. There would have been major sources of private sector money involved and indeed the nature of the tax credit program is such that the government would be paying tax credits only after the project was in place and making money.
On top of that, the project had a potential to generate sizeable revenues for the government.
I want to put on the record some of the questions that were raised about this particular project. First of all, the project investment was $470 million. All of this would have to be raised from private investors and private financial institutions. They were requesting standard Cape Breton investment tax credits for 45 per cent of the capital cost of this project. They would reduce the $800 million of corporate taxes, which would be payable from earnings over the project's life, by approximately $200

November 29, 1990
Adjournment Debate
million; that is to say, the government would realize a net gain in tax revenues of $600 million over the life of the project. This means that each $1 of the investment tax credit would generate $4 of new tax revenue. Of course they were requesting interest rate buy-downs. These are standard interest rate subsidies which have been offered by this government. This is a subsidy which the government has applied in other places, as well as the loan guarantees.
I compare the project to the Hibernia project, which we on this side of the House have supported strongly and have encouraged the government in achieving. That project was going to provide direct financial assistance in excess of some $1 billion or 25 per cent of construction costs, 40 per cent of construction costs to a maximum of $1.6 billion and other assistance, for a total federal contribution of $3,175 billion on this project.
With the private sector investment that would have been forthcoming under the Scotia Synfuels project and could still be forthcoming, if the minister would sit down with the principals and arrange some form of financial assistance and some terms which the principals would need to meet in order to receive this assistance, I believe this project would still be feasible. I call upon the minister and this government to continue to meet with the principals and assist this project.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the govemement must tell the truth to the people of Cape Breton. In economic matters, it would be indecent to give anyone false hopes.
During the ten years that the study of the Scotia Synfuels Project lasted, the federal government spent some $2 million on top of the $4 million from the private sector. Although all those reviews and studies have demonstrated that the project technology can be developed, other detailed engineering studies are necessary to ensure the prescribed volume and quality of synthetic fuel. As indicated, over the last ten years representatives of the federal and provincial governments met several times with the promoter in a effort to bring the project into being.
Since 1984, the government has spent $1.5 billion to develop the Cape Breton economy. I could mention for exemple the modernization of Sysco, the financing of DEVCO and the development of the new Louisana Pacific plant in Port Hawkesbuiy. Two weeks ago, the department agreed to provide a $24.5 million financial help to projects of Kelly Rock Limited and Point Tipper Properties under the Cape Breton investment tax credit program, while awaiting for environmental impact studies for the two projects. Together, these two projects will create directly 138 new jobs.
Some say that Synfuels is a better project than Hibernia. These projects are completely different as to size, technology and performance. From the very beginning, Hibernia has received of the private sector's financial support and offered tremendous opportunities, in terms of downstream and other benefits.
Mr. Speaker, the member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso will perhaps want to reflect on the comments of the project's promoter, Mr. Gillespie, who said, as quoted in The Chronicle Herald of April 1, 1986: "Accoring to a study completed last July the Synfuels project is feasable from a technical point of view, but not a financial one". Without a strong support from the private sector, Canadian taxpayers were asked to carry most of the project's risks. I don't think this is right, considering that the business community is not ready to do so.
